title: Start
heading: Start and philosophy
content:
This program loads, folds, simulates and fits ⁵⁷Fe Mössbauer spectra.

Recommended workflow:

  1. Load a local file (.ws5, .adt) or download it from the web database.
  2. Check the folding point and Vmax. If a NORMOS .RES file exists, it is loaded automatically.
  3. Adjust the baseline and check that the normalization is correct.
  4. Choose a model: discrete (singlet / doublet / sextet) or a P(BHF) / P(ΔEQ) distribution.
  5. Fix the known parameters and release only the necessary ones.
  6. Run the fit and examine the residual.
  7. Save the exported fit and/or the complete session.

Program philosophy:

  All parameters are visible and can be modified manually before, during and after the fit. A low RMS does not guarantee a correct physical interpretation. Always check:

  • Stability of the result when the initial values change.
  • Absence of systematic structure in the residual.
  • That the 1σ errors are reasonable relative to the effect.
  • That the area percentages are physically consistent.

Notation used in this help:

  δ = isomer shift (mm/s, relative to α-Fe at room temperature)
  ΔEQ = quadrupole splitting (mm/s)
  BHF = magnetic hyperfine field (T)
  Γ = FWHM line width (mm/s)

title: File menu
heading: File menu: loading data, sessions, web and exports
content:
The File menu groups everything that enters or leaves the program: spectra, calibrations, sessions, reports and application exit.

Menu structure:

  Open...
    What it is: opens a spectrum or experimental data file from disk.
    What it does: starts work with a real measurement; loading updates the file panel, the plot and all controls that depend on the data.
    When to use: when starting a new analysis or replacing the current spectrum.
    How to use: File → Open..., select the file and check that the folding point, Vmax, baseline and slope make sense before fitting.
    Why it matters: a correct fit depends on consistent data and initial calibration; do not fit without first checking the plot.

  Open Recent
    What it is: list of recently opened files.
    What it does: reopen familiar measurements without browsing folders.
    When to use: when alternating between several spectra or resuming a previous analysis.
    How to use: File → Open Recent and select an entry. If there is no history it will appear disabled or empty.

  Web → Web measurements...
    What it is: dialog for querying or downloading measurements from the configured web service.
    What it does: incorporate server-stored spectra into the analysis.
    When to use: if the laboratory shares measurements via web or you are working with centralised data.
    How to use: File → Web → Web measurements..., choose the measurement and load it; then visually verify it matches the expected sample.

  Web → Web calibrations...
    What it is: access to calibrations available on the server.
    What it does: retrieve a calibration spectrum or parameters associated with a common calibration.
    When to use: before analysing samples measured under the same instrumental configuration.
    How to use: select the web calibration, load it and use it to adjust Vmax/centre or as an experimental reference.

  Web → Upload JSON session to web...
    What it is: sends the saved session of the current analysis to the server.
    What it does: share the complete fit state with other users: data, parameters, components and configuration.
    When to use: after completing a reproducible fit or when you want to review the result from another computer.
    How to use: first save or prepare a valid session; then use File → Web → Upload JSON session to web...
    Why it matters: uploading the session preserves much more context than uploading only the spectrum or an image.

  Use current file as calibration...
    What it is: treats the loaded spectrum as a calibration pattern.
    What it does: estimate or verify the velocity scale, especially Vmax and the centre, from a known calibrant.
    When to use: with standards such as α-Fe or another reference measured under the same instrumental conditions.
    How to use: load the standard, select this option and follow the dialog; then apply the calibration to the corresponding samples.
    Why it matters: an incorrect velocity scale shifts BHF, δ and ΔEQ, and can lead to a wrong physical interpretation.

  Save fit...
    What it is: saves numerical results of the current fit.
    What it does: store fitted parameters, metrics and components for documentation or external processing.
    When to use: after obtaining an acceptable RMS/residual and before modifying the model.
    How to use: run a fit, check the status panel and use File → Save fit...

  Export distribution...
    What it is: saves the fitted distribution as tab-separated text (P, its σ and, in 2D, the full map).
    What it is for: plotting P(x) in another program, comparing it with other samples or publishing it.
    When to use it: after a distribution fit; also from the «Save data…» button of its dialog.
    How to use it: File → Export distribution...; see the «Saving and reports» chapter.

  Export Markdown/PDF report...
    What it is: generates a readable report with a plot, parameters and analysis summary.
    What it does: deliver results, archive them or include them in laboratory reports.
    When to use: when finishing an analysis or when comparing several model hypotheses.
    How to use: fit the model, verify residuals and statistics, then choose the output format and path.

  Save session...
    What it is: saves the complete program state to JSON.
    What it does: recover the analysis exactly as it was: data, parameters, components, mode and options.
    When to use: before closing, before trying an alternative model, or at the end of a working stage.
    How to use: File → Save session... or Ctrl+S; use names that indicate sample, model and date.

  Load session...
    What it is: restores a previously saved JSON session.
    What it does: continue a fit, review results or reproduce an analysis.
    When to use: when resuming work or opening a session shared by another person.
    How to use: File → Load session... or Ctrl+L; after loading, check that data paths and the language/visual configuration are as expected.

  Exit
    What it is: closes the application.
    What it does: ends the working session.
    When to use: after saving the session or exporting results.
    How to use: File → Exit or the standard close shortcut; if you have made important changes, save first.

title: Fit menu
heading: Fit: running, preparing and controlling the physical model
content:
The Fit menu is the centre of quantitative analysis. It runs the fit, prepares initial values, selects the model type and activates statistical or physical options that change how parameters are optimised.

General rule before using this menu:

  1. Load the spectrum.
  2. Check the folding point, Vmax, baseline and slope.
  3. Choose the model: discrete or a P(BHF)/P(ΔEQ) distribution.
  4. Fix the parameters you know physically and release only those you want to estimate.
  5. Run the fit and check the residual, reduced χ², AIC/BIC and correlations.

The menu is organised into: Fit, Fit mode (the seven modes), Preparation (centre, minima and AI), Error analysis (bootstrap, profile likelihood and L-curve), Batch fit, parameter management (free/fix, constraints, presets) and Advanced fit options.

Fit menu items:

  Fit
    What it is: runs the optimisation with the current free parameters.
    What it does: finds the values of δ, ΔEQ, BHF, widths, intensities, depths or distribution weights that best reproduce the spectrum.
    When to use: when you already have a reasonable initial model. Do not use it blindly as the first step: first approximate the centre, Vmax and components.
    How to use: tick the "fixed" checkboxes of each parameter depending on whether you want to keep or refine it; press Fit → Fit or Ctrl+R; look at the residual and the metrics.
    Why: the numerical fit only converges to useful solutions if it starts from physically plausible parameters and has no unnecessary degrees of freedom.
  Fit mode
    What it is: submenu with the program's seven modes, synchronised with the drop-down in the side panel.
    Available modes: Discrete fit, P(BHF) distribution, P(ΔEQ), P(IS) and the 2D distributions P(BHF, ΔEQ), P(IS, ΔEQ) and P(BHF, IS).
    The 1D/2D distribution modes are described in their own chapters; the two main ones are summarised here.
  Fit mode → Discrete fit
    What it is: discrete model mode with sharp components: singlets, doublets or sextets depending on the panel configuration.
    What it does: represents well-defined phases with specific hyperfine parameters.
    When to use: for mixtures of crystalline phases, calibrants or spectra where each contribution has identifiable lines.
    How to use: activate the components you need, assign shape and intensities, fix known parameters and fit.
    Why: it gives parameters that can be interpreted phase by phase; it is preferable to a distribution if the lines are discrete.
  Fit mode → P(BHF) distribution
    What it is: hyperfine-field distribution mode, and also the entry point to P(ΔEQ) from the distribution tab.
    What it does: describes broadening produced by a continuum of fields or local environments.
    When to use: in disordered materials, nanoparticles, glasses, mixtures with a size distribution or relaxation that is not well represented by a few sextets.
    How to use: select the mode, define the minimum/maximum range, bins, α and distribution shape; fit and compare several α values.
    Why: it avoids forcing many artificial sextets when the sample really has a continuous distribution.
  Preparation → Find center
    What it is: estimates the folding point or centre of the spectrum.
    What it does: corrects shifts between the left and right channels before velocities are interpreted.
    When to use: right after loading a measurement, if symmetric lines do not face each other properly or the residual shows asymmetry.
    How to use: Fit → Preparation → Find center; then visually inspect the symmetry of the folded spectrum.
    Why: a badly chosen centre can mimic changes in δ, worsen the residual and distort areas.
  Preparation → Initialize from minima
    What it is: detects absorption minima and proposes initial parameters.
    What it does: speeds up the preparation of discrete models when the lines are visible.
    When to use: in spectra with relatively well-defined sextets/doublets and a good signal-to-noise ratio.
    How to use: load the spectrum, set baseline/Vmax approximately, activate the number/type of components and run this option; check the proposed values manually.
    Why: the minima give a quick geometric hint, but they do not replace the user's physical judgement.
  Preparation → Edit minima (semi-manual)…
    What it is: interactive editor of the detected minima before they are used for initialisation.
    What it does: adds, moves or removes minima when automatic detection fails or the spectrum is noisy.
    When to use: after Initialize from minima, if the automatic proposal does not reflect the real lines.
    How to use: open the editor, correct the minima on the plot and apply; then initialise or auto-fit.
  Preparation → Auto-fit from minima
    What it is: combines initialisation from minima with a first automatic optimisation.
    What it does: produces a first working model with less manual intervention.
    When to use: as an exploratory starting point, especially for routine measurements or clear spectra.
    How to use: Fit → Preparation → Auto-fit from minima; then check which parameters were left free/fixed and repeat the fit in a controlled way if necessary.
    Why: it helps you get started, but it can be wrong with strong overlap, minority phases or very broad lines.
  Preparation → Local Ollama AI: suggest start...
    What it is: asks a local AI for a suggested initial model.
    What it does: gives an indicative proposal of components or parameters based on the spectrum and the available context.
    When to use: when Ollama is installed/configured and you want a quick second opinion.
    How to use: load data, open the option and read the suggestion; apply manually only what is physically reasonable.
    Why: the AI can guide you, but validation must come from the fit, the statistics and knowledge of the sample.
  Error analysis → Bootstrap errors (MC)...
    What it is: estimates uncertainties by resampling the spectrum with Monte Carlo.
    What it does: gives more realistic errors for the fitted parameters, especially when the model is non-linear.
    When to use: after a discrete fit that is already stable and acceptable; do not use it for clearly bad models.
    How to use: fit first, then run the bootstrap and choose a number of replicas suited to the time available.
    Why: the local covariance matrix may underestimate uncertainties when there are correlations or non-parabolic χ² valleys.
  Error analysis → Profile-likelihood errors...
    What it is: explores how the fit quality changes when a parameter is forced to given values and the rest are refitted.
    What it does: computes robust confidence intervals and detects poorly identified parameters.
    When to use: when an important parameter has a doubtful error, high correlations or asymmetric limits.
    How to use: fit the model, select the parameter to profile and check the resulting likelihood/χ² curve.
    Why: it shows the real sensitivity of the spectrum to that parameter, not just a local linear approximation.
  Error analysis → L-curve α
    What it is: regularisation scan for distributions.
    What it does: chooses an α that balances fidelity to the data and smoothness of the distribution.
    When to use: whenever a distribution depends on α and the shape of P(BHF), P(ΔEQ) or P(IS) is going to be interpreted physically.
    How to use: activate distribution mode, set range/bins, run L-curve α and compare the corner value with the residual.
    Why: an α that is too high erases real structure; one that is too low fits noise.
  Batch fit (series)...
    What it is: applies fits to several spectra in a chain or batch.
    What it does: analyses temperature, time, treatment or repeated-sample series with a homogeneous protocol.
    When to use: when there are many similar files and reproducibility is wanted.
    How to use: prepare a template model, open Fit → Batch fit (series)..., select the files and check the individual results.
    Why: it reduces manual-analysis bias and makes it easier to compare trends between spectra.
  Free all
    What it is: unticks all the "fixed" controls.
    What it does: lets all adjustable parameters be refined.
    When to use: only in final stages or when the model is already very close to the solution.
    How to use: Fit → Free all; then fix again manually the parameters you know.
    Why: releasing too many parameters at the start encourages instability and correlations.
  Fix all
    What it is: ticks all the "fixed" controls.
    What it does: freezes the model so that only specific parameters are released selectively.
    When to use: when building a fit step by step, testing sensitivity or protecting reference values.
    How to use: Fit → Fix all; then release δ, depth, Γ or the parameter of interest.
    Why: controlling the degrees of freedom improves convergence and makes interpretation clearer.
  Parameter constraints...
    What it is: opens the editor of linear relations between parameters.
    What it does: links parameters that must physically be equal or proportional.
    When to use: 3:2:1 intensities, shared widths, a common δ for similar sites or relations imposed by symmetry.
    How to use: define the relation, apply it and fit; check that the constraint makes sense for the sample.
    Why: it reduces degeneracy and avoids solutions that are mathematically good but physically impossible.
  Physical constraint presets...
    What it is: a collection of common constraints ready to apply.
    What it does: saves time and avoids mistakes when imposing common relations.
    When to use: when preparing standard models with theoretical intensities, equal widths or linked parameters.
    How to use: open the dialog, select the preset and confirm; then check which parameters were linked.
    Why: physical constraints stabilise the fit and improve reproducibility.
  Advanced fit options → Line profile → Lorentzian
    What it is: the classical Mössbauer line profile with a Lorentzian width.
    What it does: models simple natural/instrumental broadening.
    When to use: as the default and for spectra well described by conventional symmetric lines.
    How to use: select Lorentzian and fit Γ if appropriate.
    Why: it has fewer parameters and is usually more stable.
  Advanced fit options → Line profile → Voigt
    What it is: convolution of a Lorentzian with a Gaussian contribution.
    What it does: represents additional broadening from an instrumental distribution or micro-heterogeneity.
    When to use: if the lines show tails/widths that a Lorentzian does not describe well.
    How to use: activate Voigt, fit or fix the Gaussian σ as appropriate and compare AIC/BIC with the Lorentzian.
    Why: it improves models with mixed broadening, but adds complexity.
  Advanced fit options → Likelihood → Gauss (χ², data σ)
    What it is: weighted least-squares fit with the uncertainty estimated from the data.
    What it does: gives a fast, standard fit when the counts are high enough.
    When to use: as the general choice for spectra with good statistics.
    How to use: select Gauss and run the fit.
    Why: it is stable, interpreted through χ² and compatible with AIC/BIC comparisons.
  Advanced fit options → Likelihood → Poisson (IRLS, model σ)
    What it is: iterative fit adapted to Poisson counts.
    What it does: weights channels with different counting uncertainty more naturally.
    When to use: with low counts, noticeable heteroscedasticity or doubts about using σ computed directly from the data.
    How to use: select Poisson and refit; compare residual and stability with Gauss mode.
    Why: in nuclear counting the underlying statistics are usually Poisson.
  Advanced fit options → Robust loss → Linear
    What it is: ordinary least squares without robustification.
    What it does: gives every point its full statistical weight according to its σ.
    When to use: by default, if there are no spurious peaks, damaged channels or outliers.
    How to use: select Linear and check the residual.
    Why: if the model and the data are good, it is the most direct estimate.
  Advanced fit options → Robust loss → Soft L1
    What it is: smoothly reduces the weight of large residuals.
    What it does: limits the impact of outliers without ignoring them completely.
    When to use: if a few anomalous channels or non-ideal noise distort the linear fit.
    How to use: select Soft L1, fit and check that the main parameters do not change without justification.
    Why: it protects the fit without an abrupt transition between accepted and penalised points.
  Advanced fit options → Robust loss → Huber
    What it is: a loss that is quadratic for small residuals and approximately linear for large ones.
    What it does: makes the fit robust against outliers while keeping sensitivity near the minimum.
    When to use: if you suspect problematic channels but want a conservative robust option.
    How to use: select Huber and compare with Linear/Soft L1.
    Why: it is a classical compromise between efficiency and robustness.
  Advanced fit options → Propagate calibration σ (vmax)
    What it is: includes the velocity-calibration uncertainty in the error propagation.
    What it does: reflects that Vmax or the velocity scale are not exact.
    When to use: when the calibration has a relevant uncertainty or final errors are going to be reported.
    How to use: activate it before computing errors or reviewing uncertainties.
    Why: δ, ΔEQ and BHF depend on the velocity scale; ignoring its uncertainty can make errors too optimistic.
  Advanced fit options → Global optimization (DE) before TRF
    What it is: uses differential evolution to search for a global solution before the local TRF refinement.
    What it does: escapes local minima in complex models.
    When to use: with many free parameters, several overlapping components or difficult distributions.
    How to use: activate it, set reasonable limits and run the fit; expect longer computation times than with a local fit.
    Why: a local minimum may look visually good but give physically wrong parameters.
  Advanced fit options → Absorber → Thin (linear)
    What it is: thin-absorber model, linear in the absorption.
    What it does: approximates spectra where saturation/thickness effects are negligible.
    When to use: by default, for sufficiently thin samples or reports comparable with the standard analysis.
    How to use: select Thin and fit depths/widths normally.
    Why: it is stable, simple and appropriate if there are no thickness distortions.
  Advanced fit options → Absorber → Thick (saturation)
    What it is: a model that accounts for thickness/saturation effects of the absorber.
    What it does: corrects apparent changes in intensities and widths caused by thick absorbers.
    When to use: if the sample is thick, absorbs strongly or the relative intensities do not match despite a reasonable physical model. Saturation becomes visible when the absorption exceeds ~15–20% of the baseline level.
    How to use: select Thick, check the saturation-scale slider C in the panel and compare with the Thin model.
    Implemented model:
      T(v) = b + s·v − C·(1 − exp(−A_total(v)/C))
      C is the saturation scale (maximum absorption amplitude). C→∞ recovers
      the thin (linear) model. C can be fitted or fixed. In distribution mode an
      inverse transform is applied that keeps the system linear.
      Reference for the full convolution model with the source line:
        Margulies, S. & Ehrman, J.R. (1961). Nucl. Instrum. Methods 12, 131–137.
      Detailed documentation of the implementation: appendix “Thickness correction” of the user manual (Help → Manual (PDF))
    Why: it avoids attributing to phases or texture what may actually be an instrumental/sample effect.
  Advanced fit options → P(BHF): add active sharp components
    What it is: adds the active discrete components to the distribution model.
    What it does: combines a distributed phase with minority sharp phases or calibrants.
    When to use: if the spectrum shows a broad continuous part plus narrow, well-defined lines.
    How to use: activate discrete components, set their parameters and tick this option before fitting P(BHF)/P(ΔEQ).
    Why: separating the sharp from the distributed part prevents the distribution from artificially absorbing discrete phases.

"Transmission integral" absorber model (v4.18.0):

  In addition to Thin (linear) and Thick (saturation), the Absorber drop-down offers "Transmission integral":

    T = baseline − L_source ⊗ (1 − exp(−τ))

  The depth of each component is then interpreted as an optical depth, and the "Source Γ" control (fixed by default at 0.097 mm/s, the natural width) defines the source line convolved with the absorber response. It is the recommended model for thick absorbers (effective thickness ≳ 1); the exponential saturation model is still available.

New advanced options (v4.18.0):

  Per-channel integration
    With wide channels (width ≳ Γ/3), evaluating the model only at the centre of each channel overestimates Γ. This option integrates the model over the channel width (Gauss-Legendre quadrature); 1 = classical evaluation at the centre.

  Loose lines (δ extended to ±(vmax+2))
    Extends the limits of the isomer shift δ to ±(vmax+2) mm/s, so that a singlet can be used as a free Lorentzian line anywhere in the spectrum.

  Automatic global scaling (DE)
    On by default. If the local multistart ends with a high reduced χ², a differential-evolution pass followed by a local refinement is launched automatically. It removes the typical fragility of multi-site fits with strongly overlapping lines.

title: View menu
heading: View menu: plot display, themes, language and layout
content:
The View menu controls how information is presented. It does not change the mathematical result of the fit, except insofar as improved visualisation helps you diagnose the model better.

Menu subitems:

  Show residual
    Shows or hides the residual. Use it to see structure not explained by the model. If the residual is not random, check centre, Vmax, components, widths or constraints.

  Show legend
    Shows or hides the plot legend. Useful for identifying components during analysis; can be hidden when preparing screenshots or visual reports.

  Show component area
    What it is: toggles the shading/fill under each component sub-spectrum in the plot.
    What it does: makes it easier to distinguish the contribution of each component visually, especially when they overlap.
    When to use: with several active components or when preparing figures where each sub-spectrum should stand out.
    How to use: View → Show component area; select it again to disable the fill.

  Visual theme
    Changes the general Qt style. Use for ergonomics; does not affect data or parameters.

  Plot style → Classic
    Simple and familiar style. Use for continuity with previous analyses.

  Plot style → Modern
    Cleaner style for daily work and internal presentations.

  Plot style → Publication
    Style designed for sober, readable figures in reports or articles.

  Plot style → Dark
    Plot style adapted to dark backgrounds. Use if you work with a dark theme or in presentations with a dark background.

  Colour theme
    Changes the interface palette. Use to improve contrast or visual comfort. Does not affect calculations.

  Language
    What it is: application language selector.
    What it does: change the text of menus, help and controls available in the translation files.
    When to use: to work in any of the available languages: Spanish, English, French, German, Portuguese, Russian, Japanese or Chinese.
    How to use: View → Language → choose language; some text may require a restart to apply fully.

  Configure panel layout...
    What it is: opens the panel layout configurator.
    What it does: rearrange the header, file, info, calibration, reference and simulation/fit control panels.
    When to use: on small screens, wide monitors, projectors or workflows where you want to prioritise the plot or parameters.
    How to use: select a preset or distribution and confirm; save the session if you want to preserve the environment.
    Why: a comfortable layout reduces errors when fitting many parameters.

  Parameter limits…
    What it is: opens a dialog to edit the allowed limits (minimum/maximum), step and decimals of the fit parameters.
    What it does: bound the search space of the fit and adapt the sliders to the sample under study.
    When to use: if a parameter needs to go beyond its default range or you want to restrict it to physically plausible values.
    How to use: View → Parameter limits…, edit the values and save; changes apply on application restart.

  Compact parameters (no sliders)
    What it is: a switch that removes the slider from every parameter, so each one takes a single row instead of two.
    What it does: lets you see two or three components at once in the simulation and fitting panel. A sextet drops from 262 to 177 pixels tall; three stacked sextets, from 786 to 531.
    When to use: whenever you work with more than one component, or on short screens.
    How to use: View → Compact parameters. It also applies to the calibration and distribution panels, since it is an interface density preference, and it is remembered between sessions.
    Why it matters: it hides NO parameter. The numeric box still edits every one of them, with its arrows and the mouse wheel; all you lose is the slider's coarse dragging. That is the difference from a "basic/advanced" mode: here there is no risk of a parameter ceasing to exist for you because you cannot see it.

title: Help menu
heading: Help menu: documentation, version, changelog and updates
content:
The Help menu brings together documentation and program maintenance.

Menu subitems:

  Help
    What it is: opens this help window.
    What it does: consult usage chapters, fundamentals and menu descriptions.
    When to use: when learning the program, reviewing a specific option or documenting a procedure.
    How to use: Help → Help or F1; select a chapter from the side list.

  Manual (PDF)
    What it is: opens the user manual as a PDF.
    What it does: provide the extended documentation of the program, with GUI screenshots and illustrated annexes.
    When to use: when this help window is not enough and you want a complete, printable reference.
    How to use: Help → Manual (PDF); the local copy docs/manual_en/main.pdf is opened if it exists, otherwise the online version from the GitHub repository.

  About
    What it is: shows version information and general application details.
    What it does: check which version is installed when reporting bugs or comparing results.
    When to use: before sending a report, updating or verifying that the expected version is in use.
    How to use: Help → About.

  Changelog
    What it is: technical list of changes by version.
    What it does: see what functions were added, fixed or changed.
    When to use: after updating, when reproducing old analyses, or when checking whether an improvement already exists.
    How to use: Help → Changelog; review the relevant version.

  Check for updates...
    What it is: checks whether a new version is available according to the update configuration.
    What it does: keep the program up to date.
    When to use: if you suspect there is a newer version, before reporting a bug, or periodically.
    How to use: Help → Check for updates...; if an update appears, follow the dialog instructions.
    Why: new versions may include numerical fixes, interface improvements and updated documentation.

  Configure updates...
    What it is: opens options related to the update channel or mechanism.
    What it does: decide how versions are checked and from which source.
    When to use: when installing the program, changing between stable/beta channels, or solving connection problems.
    How to use: Help → Configure updates..., adjust the options and save.
    Why: a correct configuration avoids incorrect alerts and helps maintain a reproducible environment.

title: Mössbauer basics
heading: Physical basis of Mössbauer spectroscopy
content:
Mössbauer spectroscopy measures the recoil-free resonant absorption of 14.4 keV gamma photons emitted by ⁵⁷Co and absorbed by ⁵⁷Fe in the sample. The Doppler motion of the transducer sweeps the energy offset.

Hyperfine interactions:

  The interactions between the ⁵⁷Fe nucleus and its electronic and magnetic environment split the nuclear levels and give rise to the spectrum:

  1. Electric monopole interaction → isomer shift δ
       Reflects the electron density at the nucleus. It is sensitive to the oxidation state and bonding. Fe²⁺ has a larger δ than Fe³⁺ in similar environments.

  2. Electric quadrupole interaction → quadrupole splitting ΔEQ
       The electric field gradient (EFG) interacts with the quadrupole moment of the excited state (I=3/2). It produces a doublet in paramagnetic phases or a first-order correction in magnetic phases. ΔEQ is zero in perfectly cubic environments.

  3. Magnetic dipole interaction → hyperfine field BHF
       The magnetic field at the nucleus (Fermi contact field + orbital and dipolar contributions) splits the ground state (I=1/2) into 2 sublevels and the excited state (I=3/2) into 4, giving the sextet of 6 allowed lines (ΔmI = 0, ±1).

Selection rules and ideal intensities:

  For a powder sample without texture (random orientations), the angular average gives the relative intensities:

  line 1(6) : line 2(5) : line 3(4) = 3 : 2 : 1

  In single crystals or with an applied external field, the ratio depends on the angle θ between the hyperfine field and the gamma-ray direction:

  lines 1,6:  3(1 + cos²θ)
  lines 2,5:  4 sin²θ
  lines 3,4:  (1 + cos²θ)

  Special cases:

  θ = 0° (field parallel to the gamma ray):  3 : 0 : 1
  θ = 90° (field perpendicular):             3 : 4 : 1
  Powder (angular average):                  3 : 2 : 1

  The relative intensities I2 and I3 (parameters int2, int3) can be fitted freely for textured samples or with an applied external field.

Characteristic ⁵⁷Fe velocities (reference values at room temperature):

  Metallic Fe α-Fe:     δ ≈ 0.00,  ΔEQ ≈ 0.00,  BHF ≈ 33.0 T  (6 lines)
  Octahedral Fe³⁺:      δ ≈ 0.37,  ΔEQ ≈ 0.60–0.90 mm/s       (doublet)
  Octahedral Fe²⁺:      δ ≈ 1.00–1.20,  ΔEQ ≈ 2.0–3.5 mm/s    (doublet)
  Magnetite Fe³⁺(A):    δ ≈ 0.28,  ΔEQ ≈ 0.00,  BHF ≈ 49.1 T  (sextet)
  Magnetite Fe²˙⁵⁺(B):  δ ≈ 0.66,  ΔEQ ≈ 0.00,  BHF ≈ 45.8 T  (sextet)
  Hematite α-Fe₂O₃:     δ ≈ 0.37,  ΔEQ ≈ −0.20, BHF ≈ 51.8 T  (sextet)
  Goethite α-FeOOH:     δ ≈ 0.37,  ΔEQ ≈ −0.25, BHF ≈ 38.0 T  (sextet)
  Ferritin:             δ ≈ 0.47,  ΔEQ ≈ 0.90 mm/s             (doublet)

  These values are indicative. Temperature, substitutions and disorder can shift them.

title: Files and web
heading: Data loading and web download
content:
Supported formats:

  • Modern WS5: XML file with a <data>...</data> block.
  • Older ADT: plain list of integer counts without an XML header.
  • Both can have NORMOS sidecar files (.RES, .PLT, .JOB), which are read automatically.

File menu:

  Open...
    Opens local files. If a NORMOS .RES file exists in the same directory, the folding point, Vmax and initial parameters are loaded automatically.

  Web measurements...
    Lists and downloads measurements through the laboratory REST API (no scraping). It asks for user name and password only once: with them it obtains a token that is stored in the local credentials file and reused (only the token; the password is never written to disk). If the measurement has an associated calibration, it can optionally download that file too and apply the calibrated Vmax.

  Web calibrations...
    Same as the previous one, but lists and downloads the laboratory's α-Fe calibrations.

  Use current file as calibration...
    Marks the currently loaded spectrum as a local calibration spectrum, without
    downloading it from the web. Useful when you open a .ws5 or .adt file that
    contains an α-Fe or other velocity standard pattern.
    The dialog asks for:
      • Sample: name of the standard (pre-filled with the file name).
      • Vmax (mm/s): if given, it is applied immediately to the active spectrum.
      • IS (mm/s): isomer shift of the standard, informational only.
    On confirmation the program records the calibration with source "local" (as
    opposed to "web_api" when it comes from the web). The information is saved in
    the JSON session and appears in the info panel and in the exported report.

  Save fit...
    Exports a .dat file with columns: velocity, normalized data, model, residual, folded counts. In P(BHF) mode it adds a table with BHF and normalized P(BHF).

  Export Markdown/PDF report...
    Creates a human-readable report of the fit. It always saves a Markdown (.md) file with traceability, calibration, parameters, errors, areas, statistical metrics, correlations and residual diagnostics. Optionally it also creates a PDF; even if a PDF is requested, the .md is always kept. The PDF also includes the current fit figure.

  Save session...
    Saves the whole working state to JSON: counts, parameters, fixed flags, components, covariance, errors, constraints, status text. If the measurement was downloaded from the web with an associated calibration, it also includes a "calibration" block with the traceability (id, file name and calibrated Vmax). It lets you resume work exactly where you left it.

  Upload JSON session to web...
    Uploads the session JSON as a new analysis version of a measurement through the API. The "Search by file name" button finds the measurement whose .ws5 matches the loaded file (a single API call). The API keeps every version without overwriting. You can add a note, which is sent to the API and also stored inside the JSON.

  Load session...
    Restores a saved session. If the original data file is accessible it is reloaded; otherwise the counts stored in the JSON are used. If the JSON contains a "calibration" block and the current Vmax differs from the stored calibrated Vmax, the program shows a warning so that you can check whether the calibration is still valid.

NORMOS sidecar files:

  If a .RES file (NORMOS results) exists next to the .ws5, the final folding point and the parameters of the last fit are extracted as initial values. If a .PLT file exists, Vmax is read. This makes it easy to continue an analysis started in NORMOS.


CSV / velocity format (pre-folded spectra):

  In addition to WS5/ADT, the program loads .dat/.csv/.txt files with two columns:
  velocity (mm/s) and counts (or transmission). No folding is applied: the data
  are used as they are. This is the usual format of synchrotron spectra (ESRF,
  SPring-8) already reduced to a velocity axis. The file may have a header
  with #; the separator can be comma, semicolon or tab.

title: Spectrum comparison
content:
File → Compare spectrum... overlays up to 6 additional spectra on the main spectrum for direct visual comparison.

What it is for:
  • Checking whether two samples share the same Mössbauer pattern before fitting.
  • Comparing an experimental spectrum against a reference or synthetic one.
  • Spotting changes across a temperature series without opening each file.

How to use it:
  1. Load the main spectrum (File → Open...).
  2. File → Compare spectrum... → select an ADT, WS5 or CSV file.
  3. The spectrum is automatically normalised to relative transmission (baseline ≈ 1)
     and displayed as a thin coloured line over the main spectrum.
  4. Repeat to add more comparison spectra (up to 6); each gets a different colour
     from the palette: orange, teal, pink, lime, violet, sky blue.
  5. To remove all comparison spectra: File → Clear comparison.

Limitations:
  • Comparison spectra are display only: they do not take part in fitting and do
    not change any parameter.
  • If spectra have different Vmax values, line positions will not align unless
    both share the same velocity calibration.

title: Folding
heading: Folding, velocity axis and background
content:
Folding symmetrises the triangular velocity spectrum into a spectrum with a symmetric axis, halving the number of effective channels. It is a mandatory step before modelling.

What is the folding point?

  The transducer generates a triangular velocity ramp. Channels 1..N/2 correspond to the rising ramp and channels N/2+1..N to the falling one. The symmetry point (folding point) is the channel where the ramp reverses. NORMOS calls it the "Final folding point" and it is usually ≈ N/2 + a fraction.

  An error of 0.5 channels in the folding point introduces an antisymmetric distortion that is visible in the residual. If the residual shows positive peaks on one side and negative peaks on the other side of each line, the most likely cause is a wrong folding point.

Parameters:

  Vmax
    Maximum velocity of the transducer in mm/s. It builds the velocity axis from −Vmax to +Vmax. The real value is obtained from the α-Fe calibration. Typical values: 10–12 mm/s for pure Fe spectra; up to 20 mm/s for oxides.

    Signed Vmax values are accepted. A negative Vmax is not converted to positive: it reverses the direction of the velocity axis and is kept both in the GUI and in CLI fits. This matters when reproducing web calibrations or NORMOS files whose velocity carries a sign.

  Negative velocities and edge trimming
    By default every point of the folded spectrum is kept, as in NORMOS. Only anomalous extreme channels are trimmed (dead or saturated ones; see "Edge channels" below), and always the same number of points n on each side.

    When those points are trimmed, the axis is NOT redistributed between −Vmax and +Vmax with fewer channels. Doing so would artificially stretch the velocity scale and shift BHF. The correct procedure is to build the full axis with all points first and then trim the velocity axis at the same positions as the data:

      full_velocity = linspace(−Vmax, +Vmax, N)
      used_data     = full_data[n:N−n]
      used_velocity = full_velocity[n:N−n]

    This keeps the channel spacing the same as in NORMOS/PLT, and the hyperfine field is not biased by the trimming. If Vmax is fitted, this trimmed axis is scaled; it is not rebuilt from scratch with false end points.

    If the measurement was downloaded from the web together with its associated calibration, the "Status and parameters" panel and the Markdown report show the Vmax uncertainty of that calibration (or warn that it is not stated explicitly). Treat it as a systematic velocity error: it is not included in the statistical 1σ errors of the fit.

  Fit Vmax
    Checkbox "Fit Vmax using the line pattern". Includes Vmax as a free parameter in the fit. Useful if the calibration is not exact, but BHF should be fixed at the same time to avoid a perfect correlation between Vmax and BHF. The program warns you if you try to fit Vmax without fixing the BHF of all active sextets.

  Folding point
    Internal symmetry centre in channel units. It accepts fractional values, as NORMOS does. The "approx. NORMOS value" shown on screen is roughly twice as large.

  Fit folding point
    Checkbox "Fit folding point within the fit". When active, the folding point is included as a free parameter of the discrete fit: at each iteration the spectrum is refolded with the proposed centre, renormalised and the statistical weights are recomputed. Useful when the residual shows antisymmetric structure (see below) and the exact centre is not known. Start from a reasonable value (Fit → Preparation → Find center), keep few free parameters and check that the result is physically plausible; if it is released together with too many parameters it can absorb model problems.

  Baseline
    Normalised transmission level outside the absorption lines. Ideally 1.0. Deviations indicate bad normalisation or saturation.

  Slope
    Linear background (slope with respect to velocity). It compensates slight background asymmetries, but it should not be used to compensate a bad folding or a wrong calibration.

Diagnosing folding problems:

  • Residuals antisymmetric about the centre of each line → wrong folding point.
  • Persistent tilted background → badly calibrated Vmax or a real slope.
  • Baseline > 1.05 or < 0.95 → possible normalisation problem or detector saturation.

  Baseline curvature (v²)
    Optional quadratic background term ("Baseline curvature" control in calibration, fixed at 0 by default). It models the residual geometric effect that may remain after folding; release it only if the residual shows a smooth, symmetric curvature of the background.

  Cubic and quartic baseline (v³, v⁴) (v4.19)
    Optional v³ and v⁴ background terms ("Cubic baseline" and "Quartic baseline" controls in calibration, fixed at 0 by default). They complete the baseline polynomial up to fourth degree, matching the BKG(4) and BKG(5) coefficients of NORMOS. Release them only if the residual shows smooth polynomial structure that the v² term cannot absorb: they can correlate strongly with each other and with the slope.

How Fitbauer folds (and how it differs from NORMOS)

  Cubic interpolation. The symmetry point almost never falls on a whole channel, so the paired channel has to be interpolated. Fitbauer uses a cubic B-spline; NORMOS truncates to a whole channel and adds without interpolating. On synthetic spectra with a fractional folding point, the recovered linewidth bias drops from +9.5 % (linear interpolation) to +2.8 % (cubic).

  Two search cycles. The point is searched, refined in a second pass and only then used to fold, just as NORMOS does.

  Edge channels. They are no longer trimmed as a matter of course. Instead, anomalous EXTREME channels are detected —the dead or saturated ones that show up now and then in the first or last channel of the multichannel— and only those are trimmed. This is a real and frequent case: across the bank of analysed real jobs, 42 fits improved by up to a factor of 65 once detected, with reduced χ² falling from 102 to 1.45 in the worst case.

  Geometry effect. The count rate is modulated by the POSITION of the transducer. Fitbauer measures and reports it just as NORMOS does ("Geometry effect" in its .RES), but does not correct it: it is antisymmetric about the folding point, so folding itself cancels it. A relative amplitude above 1 % betrays a spectrometer geometry problem and is worth looking into before accepting the fit.

  Reproducing a NORMOS folding. Its final routine truncates the point it prints and adds whole channels, placing the axis at ⌊PFP⌋ + 0.5. To compare against one of its results, type that value by hand into "Center".

title: NORMOS (.JOB)
heading: NORMOS interoperability: importing and exporting jobs
content:
Fitbauer reads and writes NORMOS job files (.JOB). NORMOS is the program behind a large part of the published Mössbauer literature. Fitbauer does NOT run NORMOS and does not ship it: it only speaks its text format, which is not proprietary.

What it is for:

  • Opening a NORMOS fit in Fitbauer —both its model AND its spectrum— without retyping anything.
  • Exporting a model fitted here to NORMOS format, to compare there or to share the configuration.

File → NORMOS (.JOB) → Import NORMOS job...

  What it is: reads a .JOB and rebuilds the model in Fitbauer's panels.
  How to use it: File → NORMOS (.JOB) → Import…, pick the file and read the warnings shown at the end.
  Why it matters: the warnings state what was NOT carried over, which matters as much as what was.

  The spectrum loads by itself. A .JOB names its files in the first four lines, with no path: NORMOS ran under DOS with everything in one directory. Fitbauer looks for the spectrum there, ignoring upper/lower case, and if the declared name is missing it tries the job's own name and, as a last resort, the only spectrum in the folder. If nothing is found it keeps whatever was already loaded and says so.

  Keep every file of the job in the same folder. That is what NORMOS expects and what makes the import work in one go.

  NORMOS-SITE jobs (discrete sites): each subspectrum becomes a component (singlet, doublet or sextet) with its values, its "fixed" boxes and its NDEX/FACTOR/CONST constraints.

  NORMOS-DIST jobs (distributions): these are detected automatically and open the P(BHF)/P(ΔEQ) panel instead of the discrete mode. Their NSUB are not sites: they are the points of a GRID. Fitbauer translates the grid (origin and step), the shape (histogram, Gaussian, binomial or fixed), the δ(x) correlation and the edge anchors; the "crystalline" subspectra become sharp components.

File → NORMOS (.JOB) → Export NORMOS job...

  Writes the current model in NORMOS format. NORMOS has been verified to accept the .JOB that Fitbauer writes, reproducing the original theory with a difference of exactly 0.

Convention conversions (the delicate part):

  Line widths   WID is the width of lines 3,4 and W13/W23 are relative to it; Fitbauer's Γ1 is the width of lines 1,6. The conversion is Γ1 = WID·W13.
  Intensities   D13/D23 are AREA ratios and go straight into int1/int2, because the import switches on intensities by area.
  Area   DEP (or ARE) is the subspectrum area in mm/s, not a depth.
  Constraints   NDEX/FACTOR/CONST use NORMOS's GLOBAL numbering (13 + 15·(n−1)). Getting it wrong silently links the wrong parameter.

  Conventions. Importing a .JOB switches on the NORMOS conventions: line pattern from the nuclear moments (its BHF differs by ~0.035 % from the α-Fe one, about 0.01 T at 33 T), intensities by area and its relaxation rule. The job thus gives NORMOS's values. They can be changed in Fit → Advanced fit options → Conventions (NORMOS compatibility); loading another spectrum afterwards switches back to Fitbauer's, unless you chose them by hand in that menu.

Folding point: not imposed

  The PFP carried in the .JOB is the SEED of the folding-point search, not the final value: NORMOS refines it over two cycles, and in real jobs it ends up more than one channel away from what the file asked for. Fitbauer runs its own search, which is the correct counterpart, and reports the PFP as information only. To force it, type it by hand into "Center".

  Moreover, the point NORMOS prints in its .RES is not where it folds either: its final routine truncates that value and adds whole channels, placing the axis at ⌊PFP⌋ + 0.5. Taking this into account is what makes its fits reproducible.

What is NOT carried over (hence the warnings):

  • The Billard–Chamberod neighbour model (METHOD=3). DISTRI=4 is carried over. With METHOD=6, to the «Czjzek» shape: it is the same P ∝ ΔEQ⁴·exp(−ΔEQ²/2σ²), with σ² = STG² + DTQ² (checked against the NORMOS-DIST binary). With METHOD=7, to the «Le Caër» shape: the same random EFG in sextets in a field, with the same σ; NORMOS reads those subspectra from a spline file and Fitbauer computes them (if the .JOB has no BHF, 33 T is set and a warning given).
  • The Gaussian (DISTRI=2) is carried over, but NORMOS broadens its STG with the step so that P is never narrower than a bin: the width Fitbauer fits is σ = √(STG² + DTB²) (or DTQ, DTI). The import warning gives the value; compare with it, not with STG.
  • Several overlapping distribution blocks: Fitbauer handles one.
  • The LAMDA smoothing parameter. NORMOS's is absolute and Fitbauer's α is dimensionless: there is no 1:1 conversion, so set it with the L-curve. The BETA/LAMDA ratio IS preserved and becomes the edge anchor.
  • DTQ in field distributions: NORMOS ignores it there, so carrying it over would introduce a correlation it never applied.

  Watch out for inherited .JOB files: the DIST format does not accept SITE keys such as NLINE, DEP, W13 or W23. If they were copied from another job, NORMOS reads and discards them without a word, so that subspectrum never entered its fit. Fitbauer does warn about it.

title: Discrete model
heading: Singlet, doublet and sextet
content:
The discrete model superimposes several independent components (up to ten). Each one can be a singlet, a doublet or a sextet.

Component types:

  Singlet
    A single Lorentzian (or Voigt) line. Useful for phases with very small unresolved interactions or for Fe compounds with perfect cubic symmetry and no magnetic field.

  Doublet
    Two symmetric lines separated by 2 × ΔEQ/2. Typical of paramagnetic Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺ with a non-zero electric field gradient. The separation between the two visible peaks of the doublet in the spectrum is directly ΔEQ.

  Sextet
    Six magnetic lines according to the selection rules ΔmI = 0, ±1. The positions depend on BHF, δ and ΔEQ (first-order correction).

Parameters per component (prefix sN_ with N = 1, 2, 3, …):

  Isomer δ
    Shift of the centre of the pattern. Relative to the α-Fe standard at room temperature.

  ΔEQ
    Quadrupole splitting. In the sextet it acts as a first-order correction: lines 1 and 6 shift by +ΔEQ/2 and lines 2–5 shift by −ΔEQ/2.

  BHF
    Hyperfine field in tesla. Only active in the sextet. At 33 T (α-Fe, room temperature) the outer lines are at about ±5.33 mm/s.

  Γ (gamma1)
    FWHM of the narrowest line (lines 1 and 6 of the sextet, or the single line of the singlet/doublet). The physical minimum is around 0.097 mm/s (natural width of ⁵⁷Fe). The default initial value is 0.15 mm/s.

  Relative Γ of lines 2 and 5 (gamma2)
    Multiplying factor on gamma1. 1.0 means the same width as the outer lines.

  Relative Γ of lines 3 and 4 (gamma3)
    Multiplying factor on gamma1 for the central lines.

  Depth
    Total absorption amplitude. It is proportional to the effective thickness and to the abundance of the phase. Area percentages are computed from this parameter and the intensities. The default initial value of component 1 is 0.02. The GUI slider is limited to 0–0.07 to make fine manual modelling easier, but the internal fit limit is higher (up to 0.30) so that deeper solutions are not prevented if the data require them.

  Intensities (int1, int2, int3)
    The NORMOS-style convention is used: lines 3&4 are the implicit reference. That is why int3 does not appear in the GUI and is internally fixed to 1. The visible controls are int1 ≈ D13 for lines 1&6 / 3&4 and int2 ≈ D23 for lines 2&5 / 3&4. For a powder without texture the typical values are int1=3, int2=2, int3=1. DEP/depth acts as the global absorption scale.

Area percentages:

  The program computes the area percentage of each component integrated over all its lines. These are the values usually published as "phase abundances". They appear in the Status and parameters panel after each fit.

How the discrete fit is done:

  When you press "Fit" (the "Fit" button of the panel or Fit → Fit) the program:

  • Weights each channel by its Poisson uncertainty: channels with more counts (less relative noise) have more influence on the result.
  • Starts the fit from 9 sets of initial values (deterministic multistart) and keeps the one with the lowest cost, so as not to depend on a single starting point.
  • Shows a progress window indicating the current start.
  • When it finishes, writes the metrics, the 1σ errors and the residual diagnostics to the "Status and parameters" panel.

1σ errors:

  If the covariance of the fit can be estimated (well-conditioned Jacobian), the statistical 1σ errors of every free parameter are shown. They are only statistical errors; the systematic error (folding, calibration, model) is usually larger.

  If the covariance is not reliable, or if parameters are highly correlated, the errors can be estimated by resampling with Fit → Error analysis → Bootstrap errors (MC)... (see the chapter "What is new").

Metrics and diagnostics after the fit:

  Besides the RMS, the "Status and parameters" panel shows:

  • χ², reduced χ² and degrees of freedom. A reduced χ² close to 1 indicates a statistically reasonable fit.
  • AIC and BIC, to compare models on the same data: for the same data, the lower value is preferable.
  • Correlation matrix of the fitted parameters, as a colour table: rows and columns are the parameters, red if r > 0 and blue if r < 0, stronger the larger |r|; bold for |r| ≥ 0.95 (they cannot be determined separately). It includes vmax, the centre and the Voigt σ when these are fitted.
  • Residual diagnostics (lag-1 autocorrelation and runs test), described in the chapter "Diagnostics".

Quadrupole treatment "Full Hamiltonian" (v4.18.0):

  Right-clicking the ΔEQ control of a sextet lets you choose the "Full Hamiltonian (intensities + η, φ)" treatment. It diagonalizes the combined magnetic+quadrupole Hamiltonian with a non-axial EFG, using the component's η (EFG asymmetry) and φ (azimuthal angle) parameters, and computes the positions and intensities of the 8 transitions from the eigenvectors, with powder averaging. Validated against NORMOS-SITE.

Number of components:

  Since v4.18.0 the discrete model supports up to 10 simultaneous components (previously 6).

Quadrupole treatment "Single-crystal Hamiltonian" (v4.19):

  Right-clicking the ΔEQ control of a sextet lets you choose the "Single-crystal Hamiltonian" treatment. It diagonalizes the same magnetic+quadrupole Hamiltonian as the full treatment, but instead of powder averaging the γ beam has a fixed direction (θγ, φγ) in the EFG frame, given by the per-component parameters "θγ beam" (polar) and "φγ beam" (azimuthal, measured from the x axis of the EFG; the GAX of NORMOS is offset by 90°). Useful for single crystals and fully textured samples.

Which parameters are shown, and why

  Each component panel shows ONLY the parameters that can be adjusted with the active type, intensity mode and quadrupole treatment. A doublet shows neither BHF nor Γ3; a first-order sextet shows no η, φ, β, Bex, Gax or texture, because those exist only with the Hamiltonian treatment or in Texture mode.

  Nothing is lost: they reappear as soon as you change the treatment (right-click on the sextet panel) or the intensity mode, and they keep whatever value they held while hidden. Hiding them is presentation only: it changes neither the model nor what enters the fit.

  These parameters used to be shown greyed out. They took three rows per component without being usable, and with two or three components open they no longer fitted on screen. If you miss one, check the quadrupole treatment and the intensity mode first: that is almost always the reason.

title: Magnetic relaxation
heading: Magnetic / superparamagnetic relaxation
content:
The program includes two component types to represent magnetic relaxation in nanoparticles or superparamagnetic materials. They complement singlet, doublet, sextet and P(BHF); they do not change the mathematics of those models when they are not used.

1. Relajacion

  What it is: a phenomenological model that mixes a blocked sextet-like fraction with an apparent superparamagnetic doublet-like fraction.

  Model:

    A(v) = A_total [ f_block,eff · S_sextet(v) + (1 - f_block,eff) · D_doublet(v) ]

  The component is labelled as relaxation/superparamagnetic so that the doublet is not automatically mistaken for an independent paramagnetic chemical phase.

  Specific parameters:

    blocked f
      Maximum blocked fraction. If it is 1, the whole population can be blocked in the slow limit. If it is 0, the component remains a superparamagnetic doublet.

    log10 ν (s⁻¹)
      Phenomenological relaxation rate. Low values (~5) give a sextet; intermediate values (~8–9) produce broadening/partial collapse; high values (~11) tend to a doublet.

  Important: blocked f and log10 ν are NOT independent in the effective shape. Conceptually the program uses:

    f_block,eff = f_block · f_dynamic(log10ν)

  So if you release both at the same time they may correlate: blocked f reduces how much sextet there is, and log10ν also reduces it when it enters the fast regime. Practical recommendation:

    - To estimate the blocked/SPM percentage: fix log10ν and release blocked f.
    - To study dynamics: fix blocked f = 1 and release log10ν.
    - Release both only if the spectrum carries enough information, and check the correlations.

2. BlumeTjon

  What it is: a first dynamic two-state version, +BHF ↔ -BHF, with a single jump rate ν. It has no explicit blocked fraction; the collapse is governed by log10ν.

  Expected limits:

    low log10ν     → blocked sextet.
    medium log10ν  → broadened/coalescing lines.
    high log10ν    → averaged doublet/singlet.

  When to use it: when you want a model that is more physical than the phenomenological interpolation, but still simple. It is still an initial two-state model, not a full isotropic relaxation nor a size distribution.

Interpretation caveats:

  • A doublet next to a sextet may be fast relaxation, not necessarily another phase.
  • A very broad P(BHF) towards low fields may be absorbing dynamic relaxation.
  • With a single spectrum, f_block, log10ν, the width Γ and the field distribution can be strongly correlated.


3. NeelSize: Néel–Arrhenius with a size distribution

  What it is: sums a lognormal distribution of diameters. Each diameter d is converted into a volume V = πd³/6 and into a relaxation rate through:

    ν(d,T) = 1/τ0 · exp[-Keff V(d)/(kB T)]

  The total spectrum is:

    S(v) = Σ_i w_i S_BlumeTjon(v, log10ν_i)

  Parameters: T, log10 Keff, d50, lognormal σ, log10 τ0 and size bins.

  Interpretation: large particles tend to be blocked; small ones relax fast; intermediate ones produce partial collapse.

  Caveat: Keff, d50, σ, τ0, Γ and a possible broad P(BHF) can be highly correlated. On a single spectrum, fix several parameters or use independent values from microscopy/magnetometry.

4. Global multi-temperature fit

  The global fit fits several spectra at different temperatures, sharing the physical NeelSize parameters and keeping baseline, slope and depth local. It is the recommended way to estimate Keff and the size distribution, because a single spectrum rarely identifies all the parameters. It is launched from Fit → Global Néel fit (multi-T)... (see the chapter Global Néel-Arrhenius fit).

References:

  Blume-Tjon two-state model:
    Blume, M. & Tjon, J.A. (1968). Mössbauer spectra in a fluctuating environment.
    Phys. Rev. 165, 446–456.

  Néel-Arrhenius relaxation:
    Néel, L. (1949). Théorie du traînage magnétique des ferromagnétiques en grains
    fins avec applications aux terres cuites. Ann. Géophys. 5, 99–136.
    Brown, W.F. (1963). Thermal fluctuations of a single-domain particle.
    Phys. Rev. 130, 1677–1686.

  Full mathematics of the implementation: appendix “Magnetic relaxation models” of the user manual (Help → Manual (PDF))

Population polarization (Blume-Tjon model)

  What it is: the "polarization" parameter P ∈ [−1, 1] unbalances the populations of the two states of the two-level model: p± = (1 ± P)/2. With P = 0 (the default) both states are equally likely and nothing changes.

  What it does: it describes the effect of an external field, or of an anisotropy, favouring one of the two moment orientations. In NORMOS this is SPN = BHF/BSAT.

  When to use: when a relaxation spectrum comes out asymmetric and the asymmetry is explained neither by the linewidth nor by the isomer shift.

  Verification: this is Blume's two-state stochastic model. It matches its matrix equation solved numerically (difference below 10⁻¹⁰), conserves the area and does not depend on which state is called a or b. With P = 0 it matches NORMOS's Ising relaxation (checked against its executable; its OME in MHz corresponds to ν = OME·10⁶/2). With P > 0 NORMOS uses a different rule —the larger rate always on the same state, without detailed balance—; to reproduce its fits there is the NORMOS convention: Fit ▸ Advanced fit options ▸ Conventions (NORMOS compatibility), or --relax-convention normos on the command line. The same submenu holds NORMOS's other two conventions: the sextet line pattern and area intensity ratios.

External field BEXT (Blume-Tjon model)

  What it is: the applied magnet field, in T. The hyperfine field reverses with the spin and the external one does not, so the two states see BEXT + BHF and BEXT − BHF: each line shifts equally in both. It is the BEXT of NORMOS's Ising relaxation.

  What changes: in the slow limit there are two sextets (BEXT ± BHF); in the fast limit, with P = 0, the spectrum collapses to a sextet of field BEXT instead of a single line. With polarized populations (P) the collapse goes to BEXT + P·BHF.

  How to use: enter your magnet's field and leave the «Fixed» box ticked (it is a datum, fixed by default, and «Free all» does not release it). With BEXT = 0 nothing changes. The orientation of the field with respect to the beam is described separately with the intensities (I23: lines 2 and 5 vanish with the field parallel to the beam).

  Verification: it matches Blume's matrix equation with the two states at BEXT ± BHF (difference below 10⁻¹⁰).

title: Global Néel-Arrhenius fit
content:
The dialog Fit → Global Néel fit (multi-T)... fits a series of spectra measured at different temperatures simultaneously with a NeelSize component (Néel–Arrhenius with a lognormal size distribution, see the chapter Magnetic relaxation).

Model:
  ν(d, T) = 1/τ₀ · exp[−Keff·V(d) / (k_B·T)],   V = πd³/6

  Each spectrum is the sum, over the size bins, of Blume-Tjon spectra with the rate ν(d, T) of its temperature.

  Shared by all spectra: δ, ΔEQ, BHF, widths, intensities, log10 Keff, d50, size σ and log10 τ0.
  Local to each spectrum: baseline, slope and depth.

How to use it:
  1. Fit → Global Néel fit (multi-T)...
  2. Add the spectra with «Add files...» and give each one its temperature in K: by hand, double-clicking the «T (K)» column, or with «Extract», which takes it from the file name with the regular expression (by default, a number followed by «K»).
  3. Set the shared initial values: BHF, log10 Keff, d50 (nm), size σ and log10 τ0.
  4. Press «Run». The spectra are folded with the Vmax of the active calibration and fitted simultaneously.
  5. The lower box shows the shared parameters, the global reduced χ² and the local parameters of each spectrum. «Save CSV...» and «Trends...» export and plot the results.

What it is for:
  In superparamagnetic nanoparticles the blocked fraction visible in the spectrum depends on Keff, on the size distribution and on τ₀. A single spectrum rarely identifies all those parameters; a temperature series does, because each T samples a different part of the distribution.

Relation to other modules:
  It complements the individual relaxation models (chapter Magnetic relaxation): those model a single spectrum at fixed T; this dialog shares the physics across spectra.

title: Line profile
heading: Lorentzian and Voigt
content:
The program supports two line profiles (Fit ▸ Advanced options ▸ Line profile):

  Lorentzian (default profile)
    The natural profile of a nuclear transition without inhomogeneous broadening. The standard choice for most Mössbauer fits. Longer tails than a Gaussian.

  Voigt
    Convolution of a Lorentzian (natural width γ) with a Gaussian (inhomogeneous broadening of width σ). Useful when a distribution of local environments broadens the lines symmetrically without requiring a full P(BHF) distribution.

  The σ parameter is the width of the Gaussian component of the Voigt (σ slider in the Calibration box) and only applies with the Voigt profile. The Fit σ checkbox, next to the σ slider in Velocity, folding and background, allows σ to be a free fit parameter alongside vmax and the folding point; it is only active in Voigt mode and is unchecked by default. Be aware of the σ–γ correlation, which can widen error bars if the data do not pin the line shape well.

  The profile can also be changed by right-clicking on the σ slider/box: a context menu appears to switch between Lorentzian ↔ Voigt without opening the menu.

When to use Voigt:

  • Lines are clearly broader than expected but maintain a symmetric shape.
  • Moderate inhomogeneous broadening is suspected (nanocrystals, partial substitutions).
  • The Lorentzian fit leaves residuals in the line wings.

When to use P(BHF) instead:

  • The broadening is asymmetric or has structure (shoulders, secondary peaks).
  • A real distribution of hyperfine fields is suspected (magnetic disorder, particle size).
  • The Voigt does not sufficiently improve the residual.

title: P(BHF): idea
heading: Hyperfine-field distribution P(BHF)
content:
P(BHF) is used when there is not a single hyperfine field but a continuous distribution of fields. Instead of one or several well-defined sextets, the spectrum is described as a sum of many sextets with different BHF.

When to use P(BHF)?

  • Amorphous or nanocrystalline materials with a distribution of magnetic environments.
  • Ferrites with cation substitutions (Zn, Mn, Co...) that produce a variation of BHF.
  • Nanoparticles with a size distribution: the smallest particles have a lower BHF because of superparamagnetic relaxation.
  • Interfaces and surfaces where the hyperfine field varies.
  • Any system where the sextet lines are clearly broadened asymmetrically.

Interpreting P(BHF):

  P(BHF) gives the fraction of the spectrum coming from Fe ions with each hyperfine-field value. It is not directly a size or composition distribution, although in many systems there is a correlation.

  A P(BHF) with a well-defined peak indicates a majority phase with a well-determined field. A broad, structureless P(BHF) indicates strong magnetic disorder. A shoulder or secondary peak may indicate a second phase.

Simplified model:

  spectrum = background − Σᵢ Pᵢ · sextet(Bᵢ, δ, ΔEQ, Γ)

  where Bᵢ are the bin centres and Pᵢ are the (non-negative) weights.

Fundamental limitation:

  The inversion spectrum → P(BHF) is an ill-conditioned problem: infinitely many distributions fit equally well within the noise. Regularisation reduces the ambiguity by penalising rough distributions, but does not remove it. Two different smoothed distributions can give almost identical residuals.

title: P(BHF): method
heading: Hesse-Rübartsch method and regularisation
content:
The engine implements a Hesse-Rübartsch approach (the standard method in Mössbauer spectroscopy):

Recovering P(BHF) is an ill-posed inverse problem: the columns of the response matrix A for neighbouring fields are almost identical, so without regularisation the spectral noise is amplified into peaks and oscillations with no physical meaning. Very different distributions give almost identical fits. That is why the α term is added: it stabilises the solution by imposing smoothness.

Algorithm steps:

  1. A uniform grid of N_bins fields between B_min and B_max is defined.
  2. For each bin the corresponding sextet is computed (response matrix A).
  3. Weights P ≥ 0 are sought that minimise:

     residual² + α · ||D² P||²

  4. D² is the second-difference matrix: it penalises the curvature of P(BHF).
  5. The problem is solved iteratively with a non-negativity constraint.

Objective function:

  χ² = ||y − A·P||² + α · ||D²·P||²

  The first term measures the fit to the data. The second measures the roughness of P(BHF).

Role of the α parameter:

  α = 0        The fit reproduces the spectrum as closely as possible, but P(BHF) is full of spurious peaks.
  small α      Detailed P(BHF) with possible noise oscillations.
  optimal α    Compromise between fidelity to the spectrum and physical smoothness.
  large α      Very smooth P(BHF), perhaps too smooth, losing real structure.

  The optimal value is not universal: it depends on the signal-to-noise ratio, the number of channels, the number of bins and the linewidth. Always explore several α values and check that the main features of P(BHF) are stable.

The L-curve: how to choose α:

  Picking α by eye is subjective. The "L-curve α" tool in the distribution panel
  automates the choice. It scans a range of α values and, for each one, measures two
  competing quantities:

    - the roughness of the solution,  ||D2 P||   (how wiggly P(BHF) is);
    - the fit residual,               ||y - A P|| (how far it is from the spectrum).

  Plotted against each other on log-log axes, the curve is "L"-shaped:

    - vertical branch (small α): lowering α further barely improves the fit but
      explodes the roughness -> over-fitted P(BHF) chasing the noise.
    - horizontal branch (large α): raising α further barely smooths but greatly
      worsens the fit -> under-fitted, over-smoothed P(BHF).
    - the corner (point of maximum curvature) is the best compromise: this is the α
      the program proposes automatically (marked with a green circle in the dialog).

  Physical meaning: α encodes the prior that the hyperfine-field distribution of a
  real sample (amorphous, disordered, nanoparticles) is smooth, not a comb of deltas.
  The corner picks the smoothest P(BHF) still compatible with the noise level of the
  data. Still, check that the main features of P(BHF) stay stable as α moves around
  the corner.

  Important: the L-curve and the α parameter only make sense for the Histogram shape
  (Tikhonov, TV or MaxEnt regularisation). The Gaussian, VBF and Binomial shapes are
  parametric: their smoothness is imposed by the functional form itself and they do
  not use α, so the L-curve button is disabled when they are selected.

Available P(BHF) shapes:

  Histogram (free, non-parametric)
    Each bin has an independent adjustable weight. Maximum flexibility, most sensitive to the choice of α. It is the most used shape.

  Gaussian
    The distribution is parametrised as a Gaussian (centre, width, amplitude). It reduces the degrees of freedom to 3. Useful when a well-defined unimodal distribution is expected. It needs no α. Internally it is VBF with a single component (N=1, Lorentzian line): they share the same implementation.

  VBF (multi-Gaussian)
    Voigt-Based Fitting (Rancourt-Ping 1991): P(BHF) as a sum of N Gaussians over a Voigt kernel. It generalises the Gaussian shape to several components; each one contributes parameters with a physical meaning (amplitude A, centre μ, width σ) that are kept after the fit. Useful for multimodal distributions (several environments or phases). The number of components is chosen in the panel. It needs no α. Risk: with a large N there is overfitting; start with N=2–3. The width σ, common to all the Gaussians, can be bounded with “σ min”/“σ max” (see P(BHF): parameters).

  Binomial
    Neighbour model of an alloy, like DISTRI=3 with CONC in NORMOS-DIST. Each Fe has n neighbour positions (12 by default, as in NORMOS) occupied by the solute with probability c; the configuration with k solute neighbours weighs C(n,k)·cᵏ·(1−c)ⁿ⁻ᵏ and its subspectrum has the variable at «value without neighbours + k·change per neighbour». The amplitude, the value without neighbours and the change per neighbour are fitted; the concentration is an input (like CONC) unless its «Fixed» box is unticked. It uses neither the grid nor α.

  Fixed
    Loads an externally defined P(BHF) (file with two columns: centre, weight) and only fits the global amplitude, baseline and slope. Useful to compare with published distributions or to refine δ, ΔEQ and Γ while keeping the shape fixed.

  Czjzek and extended Czjzek (P(ΔEQ) with doublets only)
    The |ΔEQ| distribution of a disordered solid (glasses, amorphous materials). If the charges around the Fe are placed at random, the 5 independent components of the electric field gradient are Gaussian and ΔEQ, proportional to their norm, follows P(ΔEQ) ∝ ΔEQ⁴·exp(−ΔEQ²/2σ²) (Czjzek et al. 1981): asymmetric, with a tail towards high ΔEQ, zero at ΔEQ = 0, mode at 2σ, mean ≈ 2.13σ and a fixed relative width (deviation/mean ≈ 0.32). Only σ is fitted (plus the amplitude).
    The extended model (Le Caër and Brand 1998) adds to the random tensor the one of an ordered environment with splitting ΔEQ₀: ΔEQ/σ follows a non-central χ distribution with 5 degrees of freedom. With ΔEQ₀ = 0 it is the pure Czjzek; with ΔEQ₀ ≫ σ it tends to a Gaussian centred at ΔEQ₀ with width σ. σ and ΔEQ₀ are fitted. Near ΔEQ₀ = 0 the spectrum barely distinguishes ΔEQ₀ (only its square enters), and the report then gives no error for it.
    Doublets see neither η nor the sign of ΔEQ: what is fitted is the marginal of |ΔEQ|. It does not use α. It accepts the δ(ΔEQ) correlation (κδ) and sharp components. Compare with Gaussian, VBF or Histogram using the AIC/BIC of the report: a distribution with weight near ΔEQ = 0, or nearly symmetric and narrow, is not of Czjzek type. The «Czjzek σ» and «Ordered ΔEQ₀» controls give the starting point of the fit and receive the fitted values; with their «Fixed» box they are not fitted. It is NORMOS-DIST's DISTRI=4 with METHOD=6, with σ = √(STG² + DTQ²): a fixed NORMOS STG is a fixed σ here.

  Le Caër (P(ΔEQ) with a fixed field only)
    The same random Czjzek field gradient, seen by sextets in a fixed field: disordered magnetic phases (metallic glasses, nanocrystalline materials). The grid is the signed coupling e²qQ/2 (cover negative and positive values) and each subspectrum is the exact powder average of a sextet with the EFG randomly oriented with respect to the field. The weights are the marginal of the signed Vzz of a Czjzek tensor: P(q) = ½√(2/π)·[(3q²−2)·e^(−q²/2) + (2 − 8q²/3)·e^(−2q²/3)], with q = e²qQ/2σ. Only σ is fitted (the «Czjzek σ» control, with its «Fixed» box). Choosing it switches the fixed-field sextet on (33 T if the fixed BHF was 0). It is NORMOS-DIST's DISTRI=4 with METHOD=7, with the same σ = √(STG² + DTQ²).

  All shapes accept sharp components (by ticking "add active sharp components"). In every case the sharp components are fitted simultaneously with the distribution.

Alternative regularisation: Total Variation (TV):

  Besides Tikhonov (second differences), the distribution panel lets you choose
  Total Variation (TV). TV penalises the total variation of P(BHF) instead of its
  curvature: it preserves abrupt edges and narrow peaks better, at the cost of more
  sensitivity to noise in smooth regions. It is selected in the distribution panel.

Alternative regularisation: Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt):

  A third regulariser for the Histogram. Instead of penalising curvature (Tikhonov)
  or jumps (TV), it maximises the entropy S(P) = −Σ P_j log(P_j/m_j): it looks for
  the "least committed" P(BHF) compatible with the data, with natural positivity and
  no spurious oscillations. Useful when you do not want to impose artificial
  smoothness. It is solved with a bounded optimiser (L-BFGS-B) with an analytic
  gradient and it is sensitive to α: validate with the L-curve. The problem is convex,
  so the minimum is unique.

Correlation δ(H) / ΔEQ(H):

  In oxides and alloys the isomer shift δ and the quadrupole splitting ΔEQ correlate
  linearly with the hyperfine field H (Le Caër-Dubois 1979, Wivel-Mørup 1981). The
  panel lets you enter the slopes kδ = dδ/dH and kq = dΔEQ/dH (mm/s per T): each grid
  sextet uses δ_j = δ + kδ·(H_j − Href) and ΔEQ_j = ΔEQ + kq·(H_j − Href). The model
  stays LINEAR in the weights P; only the shape of each kernel column changes. With
  k = 0 (default) the classical behaviour is recovered. The slopes can be fixed
  (known values for the material) or refined (unticking 'Fixed'); note that kδ and a
  global shift of the grid are almost degenerate, so refine with bounds and gently.
  Applies to Histogram and VBF.

  Correlation curve in the plot: if a slope is non-zero, the distribution plot
  (Show distribution…) adds on the right axis the δ(x) or ΔEQ(x) line the kernel
  applied, with its 1σ band if the slope or the global value was refined. The
  legend gives κ ± σ: if |κ| does not clearly exceed its σ, the correlation is
  not established. The line is solid where P has weight and dotted elsewhere,
  where it is an extrapolation with no data. The «Show δ/ΔEQ correlation» check
  hides it and is remembered. If the refinement does not converge, the legend
  says so and there is no band.

1σ band and effective degrees of freedom:

  With the Histogram shape (Tikhonov or TV), the distribution plot draws a ±1σ band
  around P. It comes from a parametric Monte Carlo: the distribution is refitted
  100 times on the model plus noise of the data σ (scaled by the reduced χ²) and the
  spread of each bin is measured. It respects P ≥ 0, which the linearised covariance
  of the weights does not: with peaks surrounded by zero bins, the latter came out
  several times wider. It does not include the uncertainty of δ, Γ or the other
  global values. It is a bin-by-bin uncertainty: neighbouring bins are
  anticorrelated, so integrated quantities (area of a peak, ⟨x⟩) are much more
  precise than the band suggests. The «1σ band of P» check hides it and the choice
  is remembered.

  The reduced χ² uses effective degrees of freedom (trace of the hat matrix) instead of
