  the raw number of bins, to avoid overstating the quality of the fit.
  For more detail: chapter "Accessing options & new features".

References:

  Hesse, J. & Rübartsch, A. (1974). Model independent evaluation of overlapped
    Mössbauer spectra. J. Phys. E: Sci. Instrum. 7, 526–532.
  Full mathematical documentation: appendix “Mathematical manual of the fitting engine” of the user manual (Help → Manual (PDF))

title: P(BHF): parameters
heading: P(BHF) distribution parameters
content:
Global parameters (common to all sextets in the distribution):

  Global δ
    Common isomer shift. If the distribution contains phases with very different δ, use sharp components for each phase instead.

  Global ΔEQ
    Common quadrupole (first-order correction). In P(BHF) it is refined if its "fixed" checkbox is unchecked; in P(ΔEQ) it is the distributed variable and does not act as a global parameter.

  Γ FWHM
    Line width common to all bins. A larger Γ smooths the distribution and reduces instability but obscures fine structure. A smaller Γ can better reproduce narrow peaks but requires a larger α to stabilise.

Grid parameters:

  B min
    Lower limit of the distribution. B_min = 0 allows low-field contributions (paramagnetic phases, relaxation) to be absorbed, but may introduce artificial weight if there is no real signal there. For purely magnetic phases, starting at 10–20 T is advisable.

  B max
    Upper limit. Must exceed the maximum expected BHF. For haematite (~52 T) B_max ≥ 55 T is recommended. For α-Fe (~33 T) 36–38 T suffices.

  BHF bins
    Number of grid points. More bins = higher potential resolution + greater instability. For typical 512-channel spectra, 30–60 bins is usually sufficient. With many bins and low α, artefact oscillations may appear.

[[#vbf-sigma]]
Gaussian width (Gaussian and VBF shapes):

  σ min / σ max
    What it is: bounds on the width σ of the Gaussians, common to all components. They appear only with the Gaussian and VBF shapes and are given in the units of the distributed variable (T for BHF, mm/s for ΔEQ and IS). In the 2D modes there is one pair per axis: one for the first variable and one for the second.
    Value 0 = “auto”: no bound of its own. The fit then uses its internal limits: in 1D, from 0.001 up to the width of the grid range; in 2D, from a quarter of the grid step up to the width of each axis range.
    What it is for: stopping a Gaussian from collapsing into a peak narrower than the resolution (σ min) or from widening until it absorbs the background or another phase (σ max). It is particularly useful with multi-component VBF, where one component tends to degenerate.
    How to use it: fit in auto first; if some σ ends up at an extreme with no physical meaning, set the corresponding bound and fit again. σ max must be larger than σ min, and a σ min on its own must be smaller than the width of the range; otherwise the panel reports it before fitting. Changing the variable of an axis resets its bounds to auto.
    Where it is kept: the bounds are saved in the session and the report shows the effective ones. On the command line they are --vbf-sigma-min/--vbf-sigma-max (and --vbf-sigma-min-y/--vbf-sigma-max-y for the second axis in 2D).

Regularisation control:

  log10 α
    Logarithm of the regularisation parameter (dimensionless: α≈1, log α≈0, is the natural data/smoothness balance, independent of noise, N and depth). A value between −1 and +2 is typical. Vary in steps of 0.5 and observe the stability of P(BHF) and RMS.

  L-curve α
    The "L-curve α" button scans a wide range of α and opens a window with two plots: the L-curve (log residual versus log roughness, with log α next to each point) and the RMS versus α. It marks the L-curve corner (maximum curvature) automatically as a suggestion. A click on either plot picks another α (the nearest scanned value); the toolbar zooms both plots together, and the "Use L-curve (…)" button applies it to the panel. It is a starting point, not a definitive answer: verify the stability of P(BHF) around the chosen value.
    Reference: Hansen, P.C. (1992). Analysis of discrete ill-posed problems by means of the L-curve. SIAM Rev. 34, 561–580.

  Fixed distribution
    Loads an external P(BHF) (two columns: BHF, weight) and applies it without fitting the weights. Useful for comparison with reference results or to refine only δ, Γ with a known distribution.

  Kernel (v4.19)
    Distribution kernel selector: "1st order" (classic, perturbative quadrupole correction) or "Hamiltonian (powder)", which builds each column of the grid by diagonalizing the full magnetic+quadrupole Hamiltonian with powder averaging. With this kernel the global ΔEQ is interpreted as the modulus of the random EFG, analogous to the EXACT mode of NORMOS-DIST, and the "η EFG" control with the EFG asymmetry becomes active. With the 1st-order kernel η is ignored.

  Polarized source
    Enables a polarized Mössbauer source: the emitting sextet is magnetized (analogous to METHOD=4/POLAR of NORMOS-DIST), so the spectrum becomes a comb of up to 36 source×absorber lines with helicity selection. The controls are the source hyperfine field "Source B" and the angles "Source θ" (source-beam) and "Absorber θ" (absorber-beam).

Anchoring the grid edges

  What it is: an extra weight forcing P → 0 at the first and last points of the grid. It is the counterpart of NORMOS-DIST's BETA1/BETA2, which are added to the corners of its smoothing matrix.

  Why it matters: without anchoring, if the true distribution extends beyond the grid range, the Hesse-Rübartsch method PILES all the excess weight onto the extreme point. The result is a spurious peak that also drags the mean value ⟨B⟩. With anchoring the fit cannot take refuge there and the misfit becomes visible, which is what you want to see.

  How to use it: the "edge_pileup" diagnostic warns when weight accumulates at an edge. If it shows up, the first thing to do is widen the grid range; anchoring is the second line of defence.

title: P(BHF): sharp components
heading: Sharp components alongside the distribution
content:
It is possible to combine a continuous P(BHF) or P(ΔEQ) distribution with one or more discrete ("sharp") components in the same fit. Sharp components work with all distribution shapes: Histogram, Gaussian, Binomial and Fixed.

How to activate:

  Check the option "add active sharp components" in the Distribution tab.

  When activated, component 1 is always used as a sharp component. Components 2 and 3 are used if they are enabled ("Use component 2/3" checked in their tab). Their parameters (δ, ΔEQ, BHF, Γ, intensities) are taken from the sliders in each component tab.

When it is useful:

  • A sample has a disordered majority phase (broad P(BHF)) and a well-defined minority phase (narrow sextet).
  • Example: zinc ferrite with a broad distribution + a trace of α-Fe at BHF ≈ 33 T.
  • Example: amorphous Fe oxide (broad P(BHF)) + a paramagnetic Fe²⁺ doublet.
  • Example: glass with broad P(ΔEQ) + a metallic Fe singlet.

How it works internally:

  • The distribution weights are fitted as usual (with regularisation for Histogram, parametrically for Gaussian/Binomial, with global amplitude for Fixed).
  • The sharp components are added as additional columns to the equation system.
  • Their amplitudes are fitted together with the distribution weights, with a non-negativity constraint but without regularisation.
  • The Status panel shows the area percentages of the distribution and of each sharp component separately.

Differences between shapes:

  Histogram
    Maximum flexibility for the distribution. Sharp components only compete with distribution bins if they overlap in the spectrum. The most commonly used combination.

  Gaussian / Binomial
    The distribution has few parameters and a rigid shape. Sharp components are especially useful here because they absorb phases that the fixed distribution shape cannot reproduce.

  Fixed
    The distribution shape is predefined. Sharp components add contributions not included in the external distribution.

Precautions:

  • A sharp component may compete with a P(BHF) peak if its BHF falls within the distribution range. The fit may distribute the signal arbitrarily between them.
  • If the sharp component has a known BHF (e.g. α-Fe at 33 T as a calibrant), fix it.
  • Compare fits with and without the sharp component to verify that it brings a real statistical improvement.
  • Increasing α may transfer weight from the sharp component to the distribution or vice versa.
  • If a sharp component comes out with weight ≈ 0, it is probably not needed in the model.

title: P(ΔEQ): distribution
heading: Quadrupole-splitting distribution P(ΔEQ)
content:
P(ΔEQ) is the quadrupolar analogue of P(BHF): instead of distributing hyperfine fields, it distributes quadrupole-splitting values ΔEQ. Each term is a doublet (B = 0), the case of paramagnetic phases.

How to activate it:

  Choose «P(ΔEQ)» in the fit-mode selector. The panel becomes «P(ΔEQ) distribution» and the grid limits work in mm/s (0–3 mm/s the first time; each variable remembers its own grid).

When to use P(ΔEQ)?

  • Paramagnetic phases with a distribution of local environments: Fe³⁺ or Fe²⁺ in glasses, zeolites, clays or amorphous materials, where each Fe ion sees a different electric field gradient (EFG).
  • Materials with structural disorder that produces a distribution of distortions of the coordination polyhedron, without a relevant magnetic field.
  • Superparamagnets above their blocking temperature: the spectrum collapses to a broad doublet whose real width reflects the ΔEQ distribution and/or relaxation.
  • Iron-oxide glasses, ferritins, Fe proteins, silicates with Fe²⁺ in distorted sites.

Fundamental difference from P(BHF):

  In P(BHF) the spectrum is a sum of sextets with different fields. In P(ΔEQ) it is a sum of doublets with different ΔEQ values:

  spectrum = background − Σᵢ Pᵢ · doublet(ΔEQᵢ, δ, Γ)

  P(ΔEQ) is literally the distribution of splittings of a set of doublets.

  Advanced option: the «Sextet with fixed field» box replaces the doublets by sextets with a common field B and distributes the quadrupole shift. Use it only in rare cases: the kernel is first order (valid if ΔEQ is much smaller than the magnetic splitting) and it does not work for paramagnetic samples in applied fields of a few tesla, which would need the full Hamiltonian. The panel warns about this when it is switched on.

Physical interpretation of P(ΔEQ):

  P(ΔEQ) gives the fraction of Fe ions with each quadrupole-splitting value. A narrow peak corresponds to a well-defined environment; a broad distribution indicates disorder in the coordination geometry or in the charge distribution around the nucleus.

title: P(ΔEQ): parameters
heading: P(ΔEQ)-specific parameters
content:
Selection:

  «P(ΔEQ)» mode in the fit-mode selector. The grid limits switch to mm/s. The other controls (α, bins, Γ, δ, shape) work as in P(BHF); the kernel physics (Hamiltonian, polarised source) exists only in P(BHF) and is not shown.

P(ΔEQ)-specific parameters:

  Sextet with fixed field (advanced) and Fixed BHF (T)
    Unticked (the usual case), each bin is a doublet. Ticked, each bin is a first-order sextet with the «Fixed BHF» field and a variable quadrupole shift (which then does have a sign). Only for the rare case of a magnetic phase with a single field and a distributed ε; if the field also varies, use P(BHF, ΔEQ) 2D or P(BHF) with correlation.

  κδ dδ/dΔEQ
    Linear correlation δ = δ₀ + κδ·(ΔEQ − ΔEQ_ref), the Rancourt–Ping coupling. Dimensionless (mm/s per mm/s). Fixed and at 0 by default; untick «Fixed» to refine it. The distribution plot draws δ(ΔEQ) ± 1σ on the right axis (see P(BHF): method).

  Distribution min (in mm/s for P(ΔEQ))
    Minimum ΔEQ value of the grid. For paramagnetic doublets without an applied field, start at 0 mm/s. If the minimum ΔEQ is known to be larger (e.g. the system always has at least 0.5 mm/s of splitting), the range can be restricted to improve stability.

  Distribution max (in mm/s for P(ΔEQ))
    Maximum ΔEQ value. For disordered Fe²⁺ it can reach 3–4 mm/s; for Fe³⁺ it rarely exceeds 2 mm/s. An unnecessarily wide range enlarges the bins and reduces resolution.

  Global δ
    Isomer shift common to all bins. If the sample has Fe ions with very different δ (e.g. a Fe²⁺ / Fe³⁺ mixture), a single P(ΔEQ) is not appropriate; use a sharp component for each species or split the analysis.

  Fixed/global ΔEQ
    In P(ΔEQ) mode this parameter is not used as a global parameter because ΔEQ is the distributed variable. In P(BHF) mode it does act as the single ΔEQ for all the sextets of the distribution and is refined if its "fixed" box is unticked.

  Γ FWHM
    Line width of each bin. As in P(BHF): a larger Γ smooths the resulting distribution.

  log10 α, L-curve α, Bins, shape
    They work exactly as in P(BHF). See the chapters P(BHF): method and P(BHF): parameters.

  σ min / σ max (Gaussian and VBF shapes)
    They bound the width of the Gaussians, here in mm/s; 0 = automatic. See the “Gaussian width” section of P(BHF): parameters.

Typical configurations:

  Paramagnetic Fe³⁺ glass (broad doublet):
    Fixed BHF = 0, δ ≈ 0.35 mm/s, Min = 0, Max = 2.0 mm/s, Γ ≈ 0.15 mm/s.

  Fe²⁺ in a distorted silicate (very broad doublet):
    Fixed BHF = 0, δ ≈ 1.1 mm/s, Min = 0, Max = 4.0 mm/s, Γ ≈ 0.15–0.20 mm/s.

  Magnetic phase with a distribution of ε (advanced case, e.g. disordered hematite):
    Sextet with fixed field ticked, Fixed BHF ≈ 51.8 T, δ ≈ 0.37 mm/s, Min = −0.8, Max = 0.8 mm/s, Γ ≈ 0.15 mm/s.

P(ΔEQ)-specific caveats:

  • With a fixed field, the ΔEQ distribution may correlate with the global δ: a change of δ can be partly compensated by shifting the whole P(ΔEQ). Fix δ if it is known.
  • If the spectrum has both a BHF and a ΔEQ distribution, neither of the one-dimensional modes will be fully satisfactory. In that case the most honest model is P(BHF) with ΔEQ as a global first-order correction, or the other way round depending on which source of broadening dominates (P(BHF, ΔEQ) 2D is an exploratory alternative).
  • Area percentages are computed as in P(BHF): integral of the distribution weights plus the sharp components, if any.

title: P(BHF, ΔEQ): 2D distribution
content:
The two-dimensional P(BHF, ΔEQ) distribution is an advanced model for magnetic populations where the hyperfine field and the quadrupole splitting vary at the same time. The model sums sextets on a 2D grid:

  T(v) = background - Σᵢⱼ P(Bᵢ, ΔEQⱼ) · S(v; Bᵢ, ΔEQⱼ, δ, Γ)

Shapes: in the 2D modes the shape selector offers

  • Histogram: a free weight per cell regularised with αB/αQ (described below). Backend: mossbauer_distribution.fit_bhf_quad_distribution().
  • Gaussian: one bivariate Gaussian with centre (μx, μy), widths (σx, σy) and correlation ρ. No α.
  • VBF: a sum of N bivariate Gaussians, one per site; A, %, μ, σ and ρ of each are reported. Backend: fit_vbf_2d_distribution().
  • In Gaussian and VBF, the “σ min”/“σ max” of each axis bound the widths of all the Gaussians (0 = automatic; see P(BHF): parameters).

  ρ generalises the 1D slopes κ: the mean of y at given x follows μy + κ(x − μx) with κ = ρσy/σx, with an intrinsic width σy√(1−ρ²) around it. With Gaussian/VBF, free δ, ΔEQ and Γ are fitted together with the Gaussians, so they take seconds instead of the minute or more of the histogram. The grid is only used to evaluate them and must cover them (there is a warning if one touches the edge).

After fitting, a heat map with the marginals of each axis is shown.

What it can contribute:

  • Separating cases where P(BHF) alone does not explain the spectrum because ΔEQ also changes.
  • Separating cases where P(ΔEQ) alone is not enough because BHF also changes.
  • Detecting correlations between field and quadrupole: tilted clouds in the BHF–ΔEQ plane.
  • Comparing the marginals P(BHF)=ΣⱼP(BHF,ΔEQⱼ) and P(ΔEQ)=ΣᵢP(BHFᵢ,ΔEQ).

Regularisation:

  The backend minimises the residual plus two smoothness penalties:

    ||y - Xp||² + αB ||D²B P||² + αQ ||D²Q P||²

  with P ≥ 0. αB smooths along BHF and αQ along ΔEQ.

IMPORTANT WARNING:

  This model can seem to fit very well and still be physically meaningless. A 30×30 grid already means 900 weights for a few hundred channels, so the problem is heavily underdetermined. With too low an α, the distribution can absorb noise, folding errors, a bad calibration, badly fixed widths or missing components.

  A nice 2D map does NOT by itself prove a real distribution of fields and quadrupoles. Before interpreting it physically, check:

    • stability when αB and αQ are varied;
    • stability when the number of bins changes;
    • a residual without structure;
    • comparison with simpler models: P(BHF), P(ΔEQ), sharp components or Gaussians;
    • reasonable δ and Γ that are not being used to compensate the map;
    • compatibility with external information, for example TEM, magnetometry or known chemistry.

Recommended use at this stage:

  Start with small or medium grids, fix δ and Γ if they are known, use high α values, and treat the 2D distribution as an exploratory diagnostic. For publication, justify why a 1D or discrete model is not enough.


Current GUI features:

  • "P(BHF, ΔEQ) 2D", "P(IS, ΔEQ) 2D" and "P(BHF, IS) 2D" modes, with Histogram, Gaussian and VBF shapes.
  • Heat map with P(BHF) and P(ΔEQ) marginals.
  • “Save figure…” saves the map (PNG/SVG/PDF); the full numerical grid is written by the CLI (*_distribution2d.dat).
  • αB and αQ are chosen by hand (the L-curve exists only in 1D): vary them in steps of 0.5 and check that the map is stable.
  • Simultaneous sharp components, with free or fixed depths.
  • Markdown/PDF report with diagnostics and 2D map.

Reported diagnostics:

  Apparent mean and sigma of BHF and ΔEQ, apparent corr(BHF,ΔEQ), approximate effective degrees of freedom and warnings when the grid has more weights than channels or the effective dof is high. These numbers describe the fitted map; they are not independent proof of physical reality.


IS extension:

  In addition to P(BHF, ΔEQ), the GUI includes 1D P(IS), 2D P(IS, ΔEQ) and 2D P(BHF, IS). P(IS, ΔEQ) is aimed at broad paramagnetic doublets and amorphous materials where isomer shift and quadrupole splitting vary together. P(BHF, IS) can explore field-shift correlations, but it is especially sensitive to velocity calibration and folding.

  P(IS, ΔEQ) with doublets is NOT unique: a doublet only has the lines δ ± ΔEQ/2 and the spectrum sees the distribution of each line, not the joint one. With a Gaussian only two combinations of (σ IS, σ ΔEQ, ρ) are determined, the widths of the two lines; the panel warns about it. For the IS–ΔEQ correlation of glasses use P(ΔEQ) with κδ, which is identifiable. With a field (pairs with BHF) everything is determined.

  Warning: IS correlates with folding, Vmax, calibration offset, QS and Γ. A smooth nice-looking P(IS) or P(IS,QS) may simply compensate a wrong velocity scale or an incomplete background/model. Fix calibration whenever possible and compare with simpler models.

title: P(IS) and P(IS, ΔEQ)
content:
These distributions describe a continuous variation of the isomer shift IS/δ.

1D P(IS):

  Model:

    T(v) = background - Σᵢ P(ISᵢ) · S(v; ISᵢ, QS, Γ)

  Each point is a singlet (QS = 0) or a doublet with the global ΔEQ, always with B = 0, like METHOD=8 of NORMOS-DIST. Typical use: families of sites with slightly different shifts, amorphous materials, glasses, silicates, ferritins or samples with a valence/coordination distribution.

  Fix Γ: an IS distribution broadens all lines equally and is confused with the line width. The panel warns about it while Γ is free.

2D P(IS, ΔEQ):

  Model:

    T(v) = background - Σᵢⱼ P(ISᵢ, ΔEQⱼ) · S(v; ISᵢ, ΔEQⱼ, Γ)

  It is especially useful for broad paramagnetic doublets where both the centre of the doublet and its splitting vary. The positions are approximately:

    v₁ = IS - ΔEQ/2
    v₂ = IS + ΔEQ/2

2D P(BHF, IS):

  Explores the correlation between hyperfine field and isomer shift in disordered magnetic phases, surfaces or size/oxidation distributions.

IMPORTANT WARNING:

  IS correlates strongly with the folding point, Vmax, the isomer-shift reference, QS, Γ, the background and omitted components. A smooth P(IS) or P(IS,QS) with a good RMS may be compensating a bad calibration or an incomplete model. Before interpreting it physically:

  • fix or verify the velocity calibration;
  • check the folding point;
  • compare with discrete and P(ΔEQ) models;
  • vary αIS/αQS and the number of bins;
  • report only stable features;
  • use external chemical information whenever possible.

The full mathematical documentation is in the appendix “Isomer-shift distributions P(IS)” of the user manual (Help → Manual (PDF)).

title: Distribution warnings
heading: What each warning of the distribution panel means and what to do
content:
The distribution panel shows an orange warning when the combination of variable, shape and free parameters has a known problem: the fit may converge with a good residual, but the result does not mean what it seems to. The «More information…» link of each warning brings you to its section.

[[#is-gamma]]
P(IS) with free Γ:

  What the warning says: an isomer-shift distribution broadens all lines equally and is confused with the linewidth Γ.

  Why it happens: every kernel column of P(IS) is the same singlet or doublet shifted rigidly. Adding shifted copies of a Lorentzian line means convolving that line with P(IS): the result is a broader line, with the same shape for every line of the spectrum. A larger Γ produces almost the same effect. If Γ and P(IS) are both free, the fit can move width from one to the other with hardly any change in χ²: the width of P(IS) comes out arbitrary and changes with the starting point, the grid or α.

  What to do:
    • Fix Γ («fix» checkbox) to the instrumental linewidth: that of the α-Fe calibration (typically 0.25–0.30 mm/s) or the one that matches the thickness of your absorber.
    • Check stability: change Γ by ±10 % and refit. If the width of P(IS) changes a lot, it is measuring Γ, not a distribution.
    • P(IS) does carry information when its shape is not a plain broadening: asymmetric or multimodal distributions (for example Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺, or several environments with different δ).

[[#quad-gamma]]
P(ΔEQ) with free Γ:

  What the warning says: with doublets, a ΔEQ distribution broadens both lines of the doublet in the same way as the linewidth Γ, and the fit cannot tell one from the other well.

  Why it happens: every kernel column is a doublet with its lines at δ ∓ ΔEQ/2. Spreading ΔEQ according to P broadens each line with the same P (mirrored for the other one): for a symmetric P both lines broaden equally, exactly as when Γ grows. Only the line profile (Lorentzian tails of Γ versus the more Gaussian profile of P) separates the two effects, and with the noise of a real spectrum that difference is weak. In synthetic spectra with a Gaussian P, the correlation between the σ of P(ΔEQ) and Γ is −0.90 to −0.95, and the error of σ grows about threefold when Γ is freed; with the Histogram shape the effect is larger.

  With P(BHF) the problem is much smaller: the field distribution broadens the outer lines of the sextet about 6 times more than the inner ones, while Γ broadens them all equally, so the two separate.

  What to do:
    • Fix Γ («fix» checkbox) to the instrumental linewidth: that of the α-Fe calibration or the one that matches the thickness of your absorber.
    • Check stability: change Γ by ±10 % and refit. If the width of P(ΔEQ) changes in the same proportion, it is measuring Γ.
    • The position (mean ΔEQ, mode) and the fractions of each maximum hardly depend on Γ; the width is what is sensitive.

[[#quad-field]]
P(ΔEQ) with fixed-field sextets:

  What the warning says: with B ≠ 0 each column is a first-order sextet, valid only if ΔEQ is much smaller than the magnetic splitting.

  Why it happens: the advanced option «Sextet with fixed field (advanced)» replaces the doublets by sextets with that field, and the quadrupole is treated to first order: it shifts the outer lines by +ΔEQ/2 and the inner ones by −ΔEQ/2 (the 2ε shift). That approximation assumes the quadrupole interaction is a small perturbation of the magnetic one. When they are comparable, the sublevels mix, positions and intensities change and up to eight lines can appear: the first-order kernel no longer describes the spectrum.

  When it is valid: in practice ΔEQ must be small compared with the separation between lines 3 and 4 of the sextet, about 0.05 mm/s per tesla: 1.7 mm/s at 33 T, but only 0.25 mm/s at 5 T. With large internal fields (oxides, metals) this usually holds; with applied fields of a few tesla on a paramagnet with a large ΔEQ (for example high-spin Fe²⁺), it does not.

  What ΔEQ means here: to first order the shift depends on the angle θ between the field and the gradient axis, 2ε = ΔEQ·(3cos²θ − 1)/2. What is distributed is that effective (signed) shift, not the |ΔEQ| of a doublet.

  What to do:
    • If the field is small or ΔEQ large, use the discrete model with the «Full Hamiltonian» quadrupole treatment (context menu of ΔEQ), which does not truncate to first order.
    • For a paramagnet without a field, switch the option off: P(ΔEQ) with doublets is the right model.

[[#is-quad-doublets]]
P(IS, ΔEQ) with doublets:

  What the warning says: with doublets only the distribution of each line is observed; the IS–ΔEQ map is not unique.

  Why it happens: a doublet has only two lines, at δ − ΔEQ/2 and δ + ΔEQ/2. The spectrum is the sum of the position distribution of the first line and that of the second (each broadened by Γ), but it does not say how they pair up: two maps P(δ, ΔEQ) with the same distribution of each line give exactly the same spectrum. It is like rebuilding an image from only two projections.

  With a bivariate Gaussian it is easy to see: the line widths are
    • σ²(line 1) = σ_IS² + σ_ΔEQ²/4 − ρ·σ_IS·σ_ΔEQ
    • σ²(line 2) = σ_IS² + σ_ΔEQ²/4 + ρ·σ_IS·σ_ΔEQ
  Two equations for three unknowns (σ_IS, σ_ΔEQ, ρ): there is a whole family of solutions with the same χ². The fit reproduces the spectrum well, but the σ and ρ it returns are one of many possible ones. The Histogram shape has the same problem: the regularization picks one of the compatible maps, and it changes with α.

  What to do:
    • For the IS–ΔEQ correlation typical of glasses and amorphous materials use P(ΔEQ) with the slope κδ (δ = δ₀ + κδ·(ΔEQ − ΔEQ₀), the Rancourt–Ping scheme). That model is determined: the widths of the two lines fix σ_ΔEQ and κδ.
    • What is reliable in the map: the fraction of each site, the centres (δ, ΔEQ) and the line widths.
    • With a field the problem disappears: in the pairs with BHF (or with «Sextet with fixed field») each sextet line sees a different combination of the variables and the joint distribution is determined.

[[#thin-absorber]]
Distribution with a thick absorber:

  What the warning says: the «Absorber» selector in the «Velocity, folding and background» panel is set to «Thick (saturation)» or «Transmission integral», but the distribution fit assumes a thin absorber and does not apply that correction.

  Why it happens: the distribution histogram is linear in the weights P, and the whole regularized solver relies on that (non-negativity, α, 1σ band, L-curve). Thickness saturation breaks that linearity, so it is not implemented in distribution mode. The fit is done as if the sample were thin, whatever option is selected; the option does apply to the discrete fit.

  What it implies: in a thick sample the strong lines are flattened and broadened relative to the weak ones. A distribution fitted as thin absorbs that effect: it comes out somewhat broader, with relative areas biased towards the weak lines.

  What to do:
    • Use thin samples for distribution analysis (maximum absorption of a few per cent).
    • If the sample is thick, estimate the effect with a discrete fit in «Thick» mode and compare it with the thin one: if widths and areas change little, the distribution will be reliable too.
    • Interpret relative areas and the width of P with caution in samples with deep absorption.

title: Constraints
heading: Linear constraints between parameters
content:
Constraints impose linear relations between parameters of different subspectra. They are set up in:

  Fit → Parameter constraints...

Mathematical form:

  target = factor × source + offset

  The target parameter is not fitted directly: at each model evaluation it is recomputed from the source.

Practical examples:

  s2_gamma1 = 1.0 × s1_gamma1 + 0
    Forces the width of subspectrum 2 to equal that of subspectrum 1.

  s2_int1 = 0.5 × s1_int1 + 0
    The intensity I1 of subspectrum 2 will be half that of subspectrum 1.

  s3_delta = 1.0 × s1_delta + 0.15
    The δ of subspectrum 3 stays 0.15 mm/s above that of subspectrum 1.

  s2_depth = 0.333 × s1_depth + 0
    The depth of subspectrum 2 is 1/3 of that of subspectrum 1.

Table columns:

  Active
    Turns a constraint on or off without deleting it.

  Target
    Dependent parameter. It is recomputed automatically.

  Source
    Independent parameter on which the target depends.

  Factor
    Multiplier applied to the source.

  Offset
    Constant term added at the end.

Physical constraint presets:

  Fit → Physical constraint presets... offers shortcuts to apply common relations without typing them by hand:

  • Powder sextets 3:2:1: sets int1=3, int2=2, int3=1 on the active components (intensities of a powder without texture).
  • Equal widths within each component: sets gamma2=gamma3=1 so that all lines share Γ.
  • Tie δ of active components to component 1: adds the constraint sN_delta = s1_delta for every active component N ≥ 2.
  • Tie Γ1 of active components to component 1: adds the constraint sN_gamma1 = s1_gamma1 for every active component N ≥ 2.

How they act during the fit:

  • The target parameter is not free: it has no entry in the optimiser's parameter vector.
  • At each model evaluation the program applies: target ← factor × source + offset.
  • If the source slider is moved by hand, the target is updated in real time.
  • If the result falls outside the allowed range of the target, it is clipped to the limit.

Typical uses:

  • Equal widths for two phases with the same kind of Fe: s2_gamma1 = 1 × s1_gamma1 + 0.
  • Keeping an intensity ratio known from geometry: s2_depth = 0.5 × s1_depth + 0.
  • Imposing that two δ are equal: s2_delta = 1 × s1_delta + 0.
  • Adding a known second-order shift: s2_delta = 1 × s1_delta + 0.08.
  • Reducing the number of free parameters when correlations are strong.

Caveats:

  • Avoid circular chains: A depends on B and B depends on A.
  • Do not use constraints to force a physical result if the residual clearly gets worse.
  • A constraint that is too strict can bias the fit if the physical assumption is only approximate; in that case, release both parameters and check whether the difference is significant.
  • Active constraints are shown in the Status and parameters panel and are saved in sessions.

title: Saving and reports
heading: Saving the fit, the session and the settings
content:
Save fit (.dat):

  Exports a text file with tab-separated columns:
    velocity (mm/s) | normalised data | model | residual | folded counts

  In distribution mode the model and residual are those of the distribution fit, and the P table is appended (variable, normalised P, σ of P and weight; in 2D, one row per cell).

  The file header includes all the relevant parameters (mode, Vmax, folding, area factors, etc.) in a format that is readable by humans and parseable by scripts.

Export distribution (.dat):

  File → Export distribution... or the «Save data…» button of the P(x) and 2D map dialogs save the fitted distribution as tab-separated text, ready for any plotting program:
    • 1D: variable (BHF_T, dEQ_mm_s or IS_mm_s), normalised P, sigma_P (the Monte Carlo 1σ band, if any), the unnormalised weight and, with κ slopes, the δ(x) or ΔEQ(x) curve with its σ.
    • 2D: one row per cell: x, y, normalised P and weight.
  The header (lines starting with #) summarises the file, shape, α, χ², ν, reduced χ², AIC, BIC and the global parameters with their σ.

Save session (.json):

  Saves the whole working state to JSON:
    • Original counts (if there is no accessible path).
    • All parameters and their current values.
    • Which ones are fixed and which are free.
    • Component type (singlet/doublet/sextet) of each subspectrum.
    • Display options.
    • Covariance of the last fit and 1σ errors.
    • Active constraints.
    • Text of the Status and parameters panel.

  The session lets you resume work exactly where you left it, even on another computer.

Export Markdown/PDF report:

  File → Export Markdown/PDF report... generates a readable report of the current fit, intended for documentation or to accompany a publication.

  How it is done:

    1. File → Export Markdown/PDF report...
    2. Choose a name and folder. A .md (Markdown) file is saved.
    3. The program asks whether you also want a PDF. If you accept, it creates a .pdf with the same content and a final page with the current spectrum figure.
    4. The Markdown file is always kept, also when the PDF is generated.

  The report summarises: date and program version, file and fit mode, line profile, traceability of the associated calibration (including its Vmax uncertainty if the API provides it), metrics (RMS, χ², reduced χ², AIC, BIC), residual diagnostics, high parameter correlations, areas and percentages per component, the parameter table with 1σ errors and the full text of the Status panel.

  In distribution mode the report describes the distribution fit, not the discrete panels: setup (mode, shape, regulariser, α, grid), goodness of fit (N, χ², k, ν, reduced χ², AIC and BIC —with the same definition as the discrete fit, to compare models on the same spectrum—, RMS, lag-1 autocorrelation and runs test of the residual), global parameters with their σ, the distribution (mean, σ, mode, Gaussians), the sharp components and the warnings (weight piled up at the grid edge, panel warning). The PDF adds the P(x) plot with its band or the 2D map.

  The report does not replace the .json session (which is what is reproducible) nor the .dat fit (which holds the point-by-point numerical data): it is a summary for humans.

Automatic settings:

  When the program closes, display preferences and the last directory used are saved in:

  {settings_path_str}

Recommendations:

  • Save the session before trying risky changes (releasing many parameters, changing α).
  • The exported fit (.dat) is the right file to attach to publications or send to collaborators.
  • If results are published, always record the folding point, Vmax, fit mode and α (in P(BHF)).

title: Statistics
heading: Weights, model selection, errors and robustness
content:
This version includes several statistical diagnostics so that the fit is comparable with advanced NORMOS/SyncMoss-style workflows.

1. Poisson weights

  The folded data come from counts. For the discrete fit and the Hesse-Rübartsch P(BHF)/P(ΔEQ) distribution, the program estimates an uncertainty:

    σ ≈ sqrt(folded_counts / 2) / normalisation_factor

  The fit minimises (model − data)/σ. Noisier channels therefore weigh less, and χ² has a more sensible statistical interpretation.

2. Reduced χ², AIC and BIC

  Besides the RMS, the program shows:

    reduced χ² = Σ((data−model)/σ)² / degrees_of_freedom
    AIC and BIC = information criteria penalised by the number of parameters

  When comparing models fitted to the same data, a lower AIC/BIC usually indicates a better compromise between fit quality and complexity. AIC/BIC must not be compared between different data or different normalisations.

3. Areas by numerical integration

  Area percentages are computed by integrating the real absorption of the component over the velocity axis. This is valid for Lorentzian and Voigt profiles and avoids area formulas that would only be exact for pure Lorentzians.

4. Parameter correlations

  When the covariance can be estimated, the correlation matrix is computed. The "Status and parameters" panel shows it as a colour table (rows and columns = parameters; red positive, blue negative, stronger the larger |r|; bold if |r| ≥ 0.95), the report carries the same matrix and the PDF its heat map. In distributions, the matrix is between the refined globals (δ, ΔEQ, Γ, κ) and the mean and width of P: this shows, for example, how much Γ and the width of the distribution trade off. A high correlation means that the parameters are not well determined separately; fix one of them, impose a physical constraint or simplify the model.

5. Monte Carlo bootstrap

  Fit → Error analysis → Bootstrap errors (MC)...

  It generates synthetic replicas by adding Gaussian noise with Poisson σ to the current model, refits each replica and estimates the errors as the standard deviation of the results. It is more expensive than the local covariance, but gives a more robust idea of the uncertainty in non-linear models. In this version it applies to discrete models; for P(BHF), study the stability against α instead.

6. Residual diagnostics

  The panel shows:

    lag1      autocorrelation between consecutive channels
    runs z    runs test on the signs

  Large values suggest non-random structure: missing components, wrong folding, badly fitted Vmax/calibration or an insufficient physical model.

7. Multiple starts

  The discrete fit tries several deterministic starting points around the current values and keeps the one with the lowest cost. This reduces the dependence on a local minimum, although it does not replace a physical review of the result.

8. Progress during long calculations

  A progress window appears during discrete fits, L-curve scans and distribution fits. It shows which start or which α is being evaluated, so that a long calculation can be told apart from a real hang.

9. Calibration uncertainty

  If the measurement comes with an associated calibration from the API and it contains Vmax uncertainty fields, they are shown in the Status panel and in the report. If there is no explicit uncertainty, the program warns that it must be considered an additional systematic error.

10. Fitting the folding point

  The checkbox "Fit folding point within the fit" releases the folding centre. It is useful to correct small centring errors, especially when the residual shows antisymmetric structure. Use it with few free parameters and check that the final value is physically reasonable.

title: Diagnostics
heading: Residuals, common mistakes and good practice
content:
The residual (data − model) should look like statistical noise. Any systematic structure indicates that the model is not adequate or that there is an instrumental problem.

Automatic residual indicators:

  After each fit, the "Status and parameters" panel shows two indicators that quantify whether the residual has non-random structure:

  • Lag-1 autocorrelation: correlation between each residual point and the next. Close to 0 means a residual without memory; a high value (|lag1| > 0.35) indicates that the model leaves smooth trends undescribed.
  • Runs test (z): compares the number of sign changes of the residual with what is expected for random noise. |z| > 2 indicates too many or too few runs, i.e. systematic structure.

  If either of the two is out of range, the panel shows the warning "the residual seems to have non-random structure" and reminds you to check the model, the folding point, the Vmax calibration or possibly missing components. They are an aid, not a verdict: always confirm by looking at the residual plot.

Residual patterns and their usual causes:

  Positive-negative pairs around each line (antisymmetric)
    → Wrong folding point or velocity asymmetry. Correct the folding point, do not add components.

  Tilted or curved background
    → Wrong Vmax, a real detector slope, or wrong normalisation. Do not compensate with the slope if the origin is instrumental.

  Lines broader in the model than in the data
    → Γ too large. Reduce it manually and fit again.

  Residual peaks in the line wings (model narrower than the data)
    → Consider a Voigt profile or P(BHF) if the broadening is real.

  Systematic residual at the centre of the spectrum
    → May indicate an unmodelled component (doublet, paramagnetic singlet).

  Residual with structure in P(BHF)
    → α too large (distribution over-smoothed). Reduce α.

  High-frequency oscillations in P(BHF) with a good residual
    → α too small. The distribution is absorbing noise. Increase α.

Common mistakes:

  • Adding components until the residual improves, without physical justification.
  • Releasing Vmax and BHF at the same time without fixing either of them.
  • Interpreting the minimum found as the only possible solution.
  • Using too small an α in P(BHF) and publishing spurious peaks as real phases.
  • Interpreting the statistical 1σ errors as the total errors of the experiment.
  • Using a large slope to compensate a bad folding.

Good practice:

  • Try at least 3–5 different sets of initial values to confirm the minimum.
  • Fix BHF within the ranges known for the system before releasing all parameters.
  • Compare models with the same criterion (same reduced χ² or RMS).
  • In P(BHF), vary α over 2–3 orders of magnitude and check stability.
  • Save alternative sessions when the model is ambiguous.
  • If two models give similar residuals, prefer the more parsimonious one (fewer free parameters).
  • Always report the number of channels, Vmax, measurement temperature and δ reference.

title: Reference values
heading: Reference values for common Fe phases
content:
This section collects typical values published in the literature to guide the initial fit. The values can vary with temperature, composition and environment.

Room temperature (≈ 295 K), α-Fe reference:

  α-Fe (metallic iron):
    δ = 0.00 mm/s   ΔEQ = 0.00 mm/s   BHF = 33.0 T   Γ ≈ 0.13–0.15 mm/s

  γ-Fe₂O₃ (maghemite), tetrahedral site (A):
    δ ≈ 0.22 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 0.00 mm/s   BHF ≈ 49.7 T

  γ-Fe₂O₃ (maghemite), octahedral site (B):
    δ ≈ 0.33 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 0.00 mm/s   BHF ≈ 50.6 T

  α-Fe₂O₃ (hematite, T > T_Morin ≈ 263 K):
    δ ≈ 0.37 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ −0.20 mm/s  BHF ≈ 51.8 T

  α-Fe₂O₃ (hematite, T < T_Morin):
    δ ≈ 0.37 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ +0.40 mm/s  BHF ≈ 54.2 T

  Fe₃O₄ (magnetite), A site (Fe³⁺):
    δ ≈ 0.28 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 0.00 mm/s   BHF ≈ 49.1 T

  Fe₃O₄ (magnetite), B site (Fe²˙⁵⁺):
    δ ≈ 0.66 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 0.00 mm/s   BHF ≈ 45.8 T

  α-FeOOH (goethite):
    δ ≈ 0.37 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ −0.25 mm/s  BHF ≈ 38.2 T

  β-FeOOH (akaganeite):
    δ ≈ 0.37 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 0.55 mm/s  (paramagnetic doublet at RT)

  γ-FeOOH (lepidocrocite):
    δ ≈ 0.37 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 0.53 mm/s  (paramagnetic doublet at RT)

  Octahedral Fe²⁺ (general):
    δ ≈ 1.0–1.2 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 2.0–3.5 mm/s

  Paramagnetic octahedral Fe³⁺:
    δ ≈ 0.35–0.45 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 0.60–0.90 mm/s

  Paramagnetic tetrahedral Fe³⁺:
    δ ≈ 0.18–0.25 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 0.20–0.50 mm/s

  FeS₂ (pyrite):
    δ ≈ 0.31 mm/s   ΔEQ ≈ 0.61 mm/s

Usage notes:

  • BHF values decrease with temperature, approximately following a Bloch law.
  • In nanoparticles BHF is typically lower than in the bulk because of surface and relaxation effects.
  • Hematite: below the Morin transition (~263 K) the spin reorients, ΔEQ changes sign (from −0.20 to +0.40 mm/s) and BHF increases slightly (~54 T). In nanoparticles the Morin temperature drops or disappears.
  • Magnetite: the Verwey transition (~120 K) splits the B site into several components. Above Verwey, the B site shows a single sextet because of fast electron hopping.
  • For publishable fits, use reference values from the literature of the specific system.
  • δ values are given relative to α-Fe at room temperature. To convert to another reference, add the difference in δ between the standards.

title: Shortcuts and quick workflow
heading: Efficient workflow
content:
Main controls:

  "Fit" button
    Runs the fit with the current free parameters. In discrete mode uses least_squares; in distribution mode uses the engine for the selected shape.

  "Free all" button
    Unchecks all "fixed" checkboxes, allowing all parameters to be fitted.

  Fit menu → Fix all
    Checks all "fixed" checkboxes. Useful before selectively releasing only the desired parameters.

  Fit menu → Fit mode
    Switches between the discrete model and P(BHF)/P(ΔEQ) distribution.

  Fit menu → Constraints
    Opens the linear constraints dialog between parameters.

  Fit menu → Physical constraint presets
    Applies common physical relationships with one click (3:2:1 intensities, equal widths, link δ or Γ between components). See chapter "What is new".

  Fit menu → Error analysis → Bootstrap errors (MC)
    Estimates parameter errors by Monte Carlo resampling. Discrete mode only. See chapter "What is new".

  File menu → Export Markdown/PDF report
    Generates a readable report of the current fit. See chapter "Saving and reports".

  Help menu → Changelog
    Shows the complete list of changes for all program versions.

  Numerical entry boxes
    In addition to sliders, you can type an exact value in the box and press Enter to apply it.

Quick workflow for a known spectrum:

  1. Load the spectrum.
  2. Check that the folding point and Vmax are correct (verify that outer lines end at ≈ Vmax).
  3. Select the component type (Sextet for magnetic phases, Doublet for paramagnetic).
  4. Fix BHF to the expected value, release δ, ΔEQ and depth.
  5. Press Fit. Review the residual.
  6. If the residual is good, also release Γ.
  7. Fit again. Note the RMS.
  8. Save the session.

Workflow for a P(BHF) spectrum:

  1. Load and verify folding.
  2. In Fit → Fit mode, select "P(BHF) distribution" (or P(ΔEQ)).
  3. Estimate B_min, B_max, global δ, ΔEQ and Γ; release only those you want to refine.
  4. Start with log10 α = 0 (very smooth) and fit.
  5. Reduce α in steps of 0.5 until stable structure appears in P(BHF).
  6. Use L-curve α to guide the choice of optimal value.
  7. Compare P(BHF) at 3–4 α values to identify robust features.
  8. If there are discrete phases, activate "add active sharp components" and configure the components.
  9. Save the session for each significant α.

Workflow for Gaussian/Binomial P(BHF) with sharp components:

  1. Configure the distribution as above.
  2. Select Gaussian or Binomial shape.
  3. Activate "add active sharp components".
  4. Configure the sharp component parameters (e.g. paramagnetic singlet or doublet).
  5. Fit. The program simultaneously optimises the parametric distribution and the sharp component weights.
  6. Compare RMS with and without sharp components to verify that they bring improvement.

title: Accessing options & new features
heading: Recent options and how to reach them
content:
This chapter is an index of advanced features, indicating WHERE each one is documented in detail. Every feature now has its own chapter or section.

Index of advanced features:

  • Advanced fit options: line profile (Lorentzian/Voigt), likelihood (Gauss/Poisson), robust loss (linear/Soft L1/Huber), calibration σ propagation, global optimisation (DE), thick/thin absorber, sharp components → Fit menu
  • Kündig quadrupole treatment and Texture mode → Fit menu (right-click on the sextet sliders)
  • TV regularisation, L-curve for α and the 1σ band of P(BHF) → P(BHF): method and P(BHF): parameters
  • Asymmetric errors by profile likelihood → Fit menu
  • Batch fit (sequential warm-start) → Fit menu
  • Monte Carlo bootstrap of errors → Fit menu and Statistics
  • Physical constraint presets → Constraints

The following sections describe interface features that do not have a thematic chapter of their own.

1. Simulation behaviour

  • When a file is loaded NO model is drawn: only the data are shown. The simulation appears as soon as you touch a model parameter (slider/entry), run a fit or load a session.
  • "Initialize from minima" (Fit menu) detects the subspectra, activates the corresponding components and scales the depths so that the initial model sits at the level of the data.

2. Quick calibration from the sample box

  In the file/sample box, RIGHT-CLICK opens a menu to use the loaded spectrum as calibration:

  • "Use as calibration (current vmax & iso)": sets the calibration directly from the current velocity (vmax) and isomer shift (δ of the first active sextet), with no dialog.
  • "Use as calibration (details)...": opens the dialog with editable fields (name, vmax, iso).

3. Corrected isomer shift

  If a calibration with a reference iso is active, the program computes the CORRECTED δ of each component:

    δ_corr = δ_measured − iso_calibration

  which moves the zero of the scale to the centre of the calibration pattern (e.g. α-Fe). It appears both in the results box (one "corrected δ" line per component) and in the Markdown/PDF report ("Corrected δ" section). It is shown only when the calibration has a reference iso.

title: Command-line fitting
heading: CLI: template + spectrum → result JSON
content:
The mossbauer_fit_cli.py script lets you fit one spectrum outside the GUI from a template file (a saved session .json). Useful to process many heterogeneous files in shell loops, embed fits in a pipeline, or reproduce results without opening the interface.

Basic usage:

  python mossbauer_fit_cli.py \
      --template template.json \
      --spectrum measurement.adt \
      --out result.json

Arguments:

  --template   Template .json file. Either a full session saved from the
               GUI (File ▸ Save session...) or a JSON with just the
               model_state block.
  --spectrum   Spectrum .ws5 or .adt to fit.
  --out        Output .json path.
  --vmax       (optional) Overrides the template's vmax.
  --quiet      Suppress the stdout summary (exit code only).

Exit codes:

  0   fit OK.
  1   error (missing file, fit failure, etc.).

Examples:

  # One compound, hand-made template
  python mossbauer_fit_cli.py --template T.json --spectrum a.adt --out a.fit.json

  # Many different files, each with its own template, from shell
  for f in data/*.adt; do
      python mossbauer_fit_cli.py \
          --template templates/$(basename "$f" .adt).json \
          --spectrum "$f" \
          --out results/$(basename "$f" .adt).fit.json
  done

  # Headless server (no display)
  xvfb-run -a python mossbauer_fit_cli.py \
      --template T.json --spectrum a.adt --out a.fit.json

Output JSON format:

  Same structure as a saved GUI session (counts, model_state, last_fit, calibration, ...) plus a batch_fit_result section with:
    • spectrum, template: paths used.
    • values: final values of all active parameters.
    • errors: 1σ errors per free parameter.
    • stats: chi2, red_chi2, dof, AIC, BIC, residual diagnostics.
    • free_keys: list of fitted parameters.

  Can be reloaded as a session in the GUI or reused as a template for the next fit.

Ready-to-use templates in data_sample/:

  template_alphaFe.json     Metallic α-Fe (sextet, BHF≈33 T)
  template_hematita.json    Hematite α-Fe2O3 (sextet, BHF≈51.5 T, 2ε≈-0.20)
  template_magnetita.json   Magnetite Fe3O4 (two sextets, sites A and B)
  template_siderita.json    Siderite FeCO3 (paramagnetic Fe²⁺ doublet)

Building a template by hand:

  Easiest path: load a representative spectrum in the GUI, fit (or set parameters manually), and do File ▸ Save session... — the resulting .json is a valid template. The files in data_sample/ are minimal editable examples.

  Minimum expected structure (model_state):
    • vars            initial values of all model parameters.
    • fixed           which parameters stay fixed during the fit.
    • sextet_enabled  which components (1, 2, 3, ...) are active.
    • component_kind  type per component: Sextete / Doblete / Singlete.
    • intensity_mode  free or texture, per component.
    • quad_treatment  1st_order, kundig_fixed or kundig_powder, per component.
    • line_profile    Lorentziana or Voigt.
    • likelihood      gauss or poisson.
    • robust_loss     linear, soft_l1 or huber.
    • constraints     list of linear constraints (optional).

  The folding center is NOT taken from the template: each spectrum auto-detects its own. vmax is (calibration); can be overridden with --vmax.


Complete reference:

  The full list of options of both command-line tools (mossbauer_fit_cli.py for discrete fits and fit_bhf_distribution_cli.py for distributions, including NORMOS conventions, kernel physics and 2D shapes) is in the appendix “Command-line tools” of the user manual (Help → Manual (PDF)).

title: What is new
heading: Changes and new features since version 0.2
content:
This chapter lists the features added in each version. The installed version is shown in Help → About; the full technical history is in Help → Changelog.

Features accumulated up to v0.2.6 (described in their own chapters):

  • Poisson-weighted discrete fit (automatic) → Statistics
  • Reduced χ², AIC and BIC → Statistics
  • Areas by numerical integration (valid for Lorentzian and Voigt) → Statistics
  • Colour correlation matrix (also in distributions) → Statistics
  • Extended L-curve: automatic corner and one-click choice of α → P(BHF): parameters
  • Residual diagnostics (lag-1, runs test) → Diagnostics
  • Deterministic multistart (9 starts, automatic) → Statistics
  • Markdown/PDF report → Saving and reports
  • Progress windows for long calculations (automatic)
  • Poisson-weighted P(BHF)/P(ΔEQ) distributions (automatic)
  • Monte Carlo bootstrap of errors → Fit menu and Statistics (see the steps below)
  • Physical constraint presets → Constraints (see the steps below)
  • Folding point fitted as a free parameter → Folding
  • Vmax calibration uncertainty warning in the Status panel and the report

How to use the Monte Carlo bootstrap (Fit → Error analysis → Bootstrap errors (MC)...):

  1. Load the spectrum and do a discrete fit, leaving the desired parameters free.
  2. Open Fit → Error analysis → Bootstrap errors (MC)...
  3. Enter the number of replicas (30 by default; between 5 and 300). More replicas = a more stable error but more time.
  4. The program generates synthetic spectra by adding Poisson noise to the fitted model and refits each one.
  5. The standard deviation across replicas replaces the 1σ error in the Status panel.
  Only available in discrete mode; for P(BHF)/P(ΔEQ) study the stability by varying α.

How to use the physical presets (Fit → Physical constraint presets...):

  They act only on the active components:

  • "Powder sextets 3:2:1": sets the intensities to the ratio of a powder without texture (int1=3, int2=2, int3=1).
  • "Equal widths within each component": sets Γ2=Γ3=1 (lines 2-5 and 3-4 equal to the outer ones).
  • "Tie δ of active components to component 1": δN=δ1 for every active component N ≥ 2.
  • "Tie Γ1 of active components to component 1": Γ1,N=Γ1,1 for every active component N ≥ 2.
  The added constraints can be reviewed in Fit → Parameter constraints...

v0.4.2 — Calibration from a local file:
  File → "Use current file as calibration...": registers the loaded spectrum as a local velocity standard (source="local") without downloading it from the web. The information persists in the JSON session.

v0.4.3 — Display of the active calibration:
  Permanent label under the file name: shows the active calibration, Vmax and IS at all times. The calibration dialog pre-fills Vmax and the δ of the first active sextet automatically.

v0.4.4 — Calibration persists across files:
  The active calibration no longer disappears when a new file is opened. It persists until the user explicitly sets another one.

v0.4.5 — Extended BHF and ΔEQ ranges:
  BHF up to 60 T in sextets and distributions. ΔEQ goes from [0, 4] to [−4, 4] mm/s, allowing negative electric field gradients.

v0.4.6 — Sample data and improved filter:
  data_sample/ includes spectra and fit sessions ready to open. The dialog accepts *.WS5 and *.ADT in upper case (useful on Windows).

v0.4.7 — Automatic pip on update and at startup:
  After an update the program runs pip install -r requirements.txt automatically. At startup it also does so in the background if requirements.txt changed.

v0.4.8 — Line profile from the σ slider:
  Right-click the σ slider to switch between Lorentzian and Voigt without going to the menu.

v0.4.9 — Asymmetric profile-likelihood errors:
  Fit → Error analysis → Profile-likelihood errors... profiles Δχ²(p) for each free parameter and locates the Δχ²=1 (1σ) and Δχ²=4 (2σ) crossings. Asymmetric +Δ⁺/−Δ⁻ bars in the Status panel, the report and a plot of the curves. See Fit menu.

v0.4.10 — Batch fit (sequential warm-start):
  Fit → Batch fit (series)... Select N files and fit them one by one, using the active model as a template and the result of the previous one as the start. Optional extraction of a metadata value from the name with a regex (?P<v>...). TSV export and a trends window. See Fit menu.

v0.4.11 — NORMOS compatibility and velocity axis:
  Vmax accepts a sign and keeps it in the GUI, the CLI and web calibrations. int3 hidden and fixed to 1 (NORMOS convention; int1≈D13, int2≈D23). Initial depth 0.02, Γ = 0.15 mm/s. When edge channels are trimmed, the original velocity axis is trimmed too (it is not rebuilt to ±Vmax), avoiding a bias in BHF.


v4.9.0 — Hybrid CWT detection, comparison and spectrum library:

  • Visual spectrum comparison: File → Compare spectrum... overlays up to 6
    additional spectra for direct comparison → Spectrum comparison
  • Global Néel-Arrhenius fit: Fit → Global Néel fit (multi-T)... shares Keff,
    sizes and τ₀ across a series of spectra at different T → Global Néel-Arrhenius fit
  • Hybrid CWT detection: the automatic start uses multi-scale CWT with a Ricker
    wavelet (0.12–2.0 mm/s) + a direct channel for narrow doublets. More robust on
    sextets and overlapping lines.
  • Early stop in the multistart: the fit stops if the cost does not improve by more
    than 1 ppm in 4 consecutive starts, without loss of quality.
  • CSV/velocity format: pre-folded spectra with velocity/counts columns
    (ESRF, synchrotron) → Files and web
  • Library of 10 synthetic reference spectra in data_sample/public/:
    goethite, ferrihydrite, pyrite, troilite, wüstite, ilmenite, jarosite,
    lepidocrocite, maghemite and pyrrhotite, with their fit templates.
